blocks.text: King Charles has referred a landmark slavery reparations petition from Jamaica to a high-level UK appeals court for legal advice, Jamaica’s culture minister announced in parliament on Tuesday.

Referring to the move as a “really big deal”, Olivia Grange told Jamaica’s MPs the monarch had confirmed that their legal questions have been passed on to the London-based privy council – the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.

The petition seeks guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences.

“Indeed we went fearless and boldly into this chapter when we petitioned the king on Monday, September 7, 2026 – one day after the 245th anniversary of the commemoration of the Zong massacre, an event that captures the barbarity of chattel enslavement,” Grange said in parliament.

“The king could have ignored us. The king could have delayed responding to us. The king could have made a decision not to refer the questions to the privy council, or he could make a decision to refer the questions,” she said, before adding “King Charles has referred the petition filed on the 7th of September, 2026, on behalf of the people of Jamaica to the Judicial Committee of the privy council.”

Jamaica had activated a rarely used mechanism in the Judicial Committee Act 1833, which allows the king to refer questions of “legal or constitutional nature” to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts, according to the country’s legal counsels.
The minister said that taking the matter to the International Court of Justice, was not an option for Jamaica.

“The United Kingdom has placed specific reservations on the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ which prevent the Court from adjudicating on disputes between the United Kingdom and the government of any other country which is or has been a Member of the Commonwealth”.

A privy council opinion would not compel the UK government to pay reparations, but Jamaican officials believe it could shape negotiations and legal options and set a precedent for other Commonwealth nations seeking reparations.

Earlier this month, Grange led a Jamaican delegation to London to officially lodge the petition. While in the UK, the group, lawyers and members of the country’s national council on reparation met diaspora communities, MPs, church leaders and cultural institutions – among them the British Museum, from which Jamaica is seeking the return of artefacts taken during colonial rule.

Tuesday’s announcement follows the Caricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place in Barbados last week. Officials at the conference said that Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal.

Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options.

Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the CRC, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today.

He said: “When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?”
Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”.

Grange told parliament that the country is “awaiting directions from the Judicial Committee of the privy council as to the next steps to be taken in the case. And the attorney general is preparing to deal with the case”.

articles.title: Fact check: Viral airport photo does not show Duterte back in Philippines
articles.summary: A viral AI-generated photo falsely shows Rodrigo Duterte back in the Philippines with his family.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 9:11am
An AI-generated image of former President Rodrigo Duterte with his family at an airport circulated on social media.
MANILA, Philippines — A viral image purporting to show former President Rodrigo Duterte with members of his family at an airport falsely claims that he has returned to the Philippines.

The image, which appears to use Duterte's appearance during his recent International Criminal Court (ICC) hearing, shows him alongside Vice President Sara Duterte, Honeylet Avanceña, Davao City Rep. Paolo "Pulong" Duterte and Veronica "Kitty" Duterte.
Two Facebook posts shared the image with captions claiming that the former president had returned to the Philippines.
Facebook posts shared the AI-generated image with captions claiming that former President Rodrigo Duterte had returned to the Philippines.
Screenshot taken Sept. 22, 2026, 12:30 p.m.

One post was published on September 17, while another was posted on September 19, days after Duterte made his first in-person appearance before the ICC on September 16. He had previously appeared before the court via video link during his initial appearance in March 2025.
One post's caption read:
magagalit na naman si ante kler nito ???? tatay digong pauwi na ng pilipinas ????????
The image also circulated on TikTok, where some posts garnered thousands of views.
TikTok posts similarly shared the image with claims that Duterte had returned to the Philippines.
TikTok posts also shared the AI-generated image claiming that former President Rodrigo Duterte had returned to the Philippines.
Rating: This is fake.
Facts

Duterte has not returned to the Philippines. He remains in ICC custody in The Hague, Netherlands. On September 16, Trial Chamber III ordered that he continue to be detained after finding "no notable change" in circumstances that would warrant his release, with or without conditions.
The chamber said the prospect of Duterte facing trial, and a lengthy prison sentence if convicted, had increased the risk of him absconding or obstructing or endangering court proceedings.

As of the September 16 detention ruling, the chamber's decision on Duterte's fitness to stand trial remained pending. The judges said reports submitted by a panel of three court-appointed medical experts did not contain information warranting a change in his detention.

“The Chamber finds that the prospect of the Accused facing a trial, and (in the event of a conviction), a lengthy prison sentence, has increased. There is, therefore, a likelihood of the Accused absconding and/or obstructing or endangering the investigation or the court proceedings,” the five-page decision read.
Duterte's trial is scheduled to open on November 30. The ICC confirmed in April three counts of crimes against humanity brought against him and committed him to trial.
Why we fact-checked this
The viral photo is one of several AI-generated images and videos of Duterte that have circulated since his appearance at the ICC, with one video claiming to show Duterte thanking his supporters.

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appears at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on September 16, 2026, during a preparatory session as he faces charges over his “war on drugs,” which killed thousands.
AFP / Pool / Piroschka Van De Wouw

Duterte appeared in person at the ICC for the first time on September 16 for the third status conference in his case. He only previously appeared before the court via videolink during his initial appearance in March 2025.
The former president’s trial is scheduled to open on November 30, as he faces three counts of crimes against humanity over his administration’s war on drugs.

As of September 22, one of the Facebook posts has garnered more than 2,800 reactions, 300 comments, and 100 shares, while the other has obtained more than 2,100 reactions, 250 comments, and 100 shares.
One of the TikTok videos, meanwhile, has garnered more than 400,000 views, 19,600 likes, and 500 comments, while the other has gained at least 73,000 views, 5,000 likes, and 300 comments.

articles.title: Qantas announces 18-hour direct flights from Sydney to New York
articles.summary: Flying from 2028, it’s the national carrier’s second ultra long-haul route after Sydney to London direct takes off in 2027

blocks.text: Travellers will be able to fly between Sydney and New York in just 18 hours from mid-2028 when Qantas launches its second ultra long-haul route, cutting at least three hours from the travel time.
The route will be the second in Qantas’ Project Sunrise expansion plans, after new Sydney to London direct flights to begin in October 2027.

It would be the first commercial direct flight from Kingsford-Smith airport to New York’s JFK airport. Qantas currently offers flights from Sydney to New York with a stopover in Los Angeles, which take 21 hours and typically cost more than $1,400 one way or more than $1,900 return.
Qantas has not disclosed prices for the Project Sunrise routes. It has previously suggested direct fares could cost 20% more than stopover fares and said ticket prices are facing upward pressure.

Tickets for the Sydney to New York route are set to go on sale in August 2027, Qantas said. It has not specified which month flights will begin. When it announced the London route launch date, the company said it would reveal launch timings in 2027.
Qantas is planning to unveil more 20-hour direct flights from Perth in future but has abandoned references to previous hopes to run routes from Brisbane or Melbourne.
The company has ordered 12 Airbus A350–1000ULRs, fitted with extra fuel tanks, which can fly over 16,000km and up to 22 hours nonstop. The first is expected to arrive in Australia in April 2027.

The planes were specifically designed to fly up to 22 hours nonstop for Qantas, to complete some of the longest commercial flights in the world. A test model in July completed a 24-hour, 24-minute flight from Melbourne to Airbus’ manufacturing facility in Toulouse, France, believed to be the longest-ever commercial flight.

Each plane will contain a dedicated “wellbeing zone” between the economy and premium economy cabins, where passengers will be able to stretch, watch guided exercise videos and help themselves to snacks and drinks.
Only 140 of the A350–1000ULR’s 238 seats are standard economy. It contains six first-class suites, 52 business suites and 40 premium economy seats.
after newsletter promotion

The company expects the Project Sunrise flights and sustained premium flight demand to increase its earnings by $400m over the next five years, with profit margins to rise from today’s rate of 4% to 10%.

Qantas said demand for its flights in and out of New York have doubled since 2023. Short-term US arrivals to Australia picked up 4% in the year to July 2026 compared with the year prior, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
However, Australians travelling and returning from the US dropped 9% in the same period.
Qantas’ chief executive, Vanessa Hudson, said the flights could change the way Australians travel.

‘“Reaching New York non-stop completes a vision we set out many years ago, and it’s a moment of enormous pride for the thousands of our people who have been working hard to make Project Sunrise a reality,” she said.

The company is training pilots on its A350 simulator and is teaching engineers about the new aircraft. The company says more than 360 pilots and 1,200 cabin crew will be trained to operate the aircraft by the time the entire fleet has arrived.

articles.title: Trump threatens to annihilate Iran as diplomats push for deal at UN
articles.summary: The ongoing conflict has implications for global oil markets and regional security, with Gulf states seeking a security framework involving Iran, amid rising energy costs and political pressures in…

blocks.text: SIDELINES. US President Donald Trump participates in a Shield of the Americas event on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City, US, September 22, 2026.

The ongoing conflict has implications for global oil markets and regional security, with Gulf states seeking a security framework involving Iran, amid rising energy costs and political pressures in the US

items: US President Donald Trump warned of potential annihilation of Iran if no deal is reached, while also suggesting that diplomatic efforts are underway to resolve the conflict.
Iran dismissed Trump's comments as propaganda and indicated readiness to respond aggressively to US actions, while also engaging in discussions with Qatar to de-escalate tensions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

UNITED NATIONS – US President Donald Trump warned on Tuesday, September 22, that he could annihilate Iran if there is no deal to end the war, but also suggested an agreement could come soon amid a diplomatic push at the United Nations.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said in a speech at the UN General Assembly in New York.

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?… Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”

blocks.caption: Tehran hints at Hormuz talks with US as leaders gather at UN

blocks.text: In a statement on Tuesday, Iran’s Armed Forces dismissed Trump’s comments at the UN as “propaganda”, saying their response is “full readiness to inflict more severe, crushing, and unpredictable blows on the aggressors.”

But away from the fiery rhetoric, discussions continued to try to end the nearly seven-month conflict that began with joint US-Israeli strikes and has since killed thousands, driven up oil prices and drawn in neighboring countries.
Trump said that envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner “had a very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran.”
“I think there’s a lot of momentum for them to make a deal,” he said.

Trump also met the leaders of Middle Eastern countries who are keen to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of global oil and gas shipments before the war, but are wary of giving their longstanding rival Iran too much power.
Many also host huge US military bases that have come under repeated Iranian attack throughout the war.
“We think that the situation with Iran could end right after the (November 3) midterm elections, maybe before. I don’t know. You never know,” Trump said as he met the leaders.

The diplomatic maneuvering comes as Trump faces pressure on multiple fronts — rising energy costs at home, a widening regional conflict abroad, and the midterms six weeks away that could reshape his political standing. Whether talks produce a deal or the war escalates further carries consequences for global oil markets, Gulf security and millions of Iranians.

Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araqchi met with Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani of Qatar, which has spent months trying to de-escalate the conflict, the Qatari state news agency reported.
A senior Iranian official said Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the US eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.

The senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had conveyed its latest proposal to Washington through mediators last week and could reopen the strait to Gulf shipping within seven days if its demands were met.

In a reminder of Iran’s firm position so far, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who headed Iran’s negotiating team at previous talks, said Iran would never surrender: “Trump must understand that he cannot impose his power on the Iranian people and its armed forces.”

On the table at the Gulf states’ meeting with Trump is a Qatari proposal for a common security framework involving Iran and the Arab Gulf states, regional sources said. One source said Iran was reviewing the proposal.
Al Thani has said any such arrangement would need to provide security guarantees for the Gulf states and expand economic interdependence with Iran.

Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, has been drawn deeper into the war this month as Iran-aligned Houthi fighters have advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.

The US, which bombed the Houthis for two months last year, has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to rejoin the fight. The New York Times reported that Trump called off US strikes against the Houthis on Sunday at the last minute.

Asked why Washington had held back from striking the Houthis, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States would always support Saudi Arabia, adding:“That said, that is a very dangerous and complex conflict that pre-exists … We have a history with the Houthis as well, and that’s something we don’t want to see impacted either.”

Oil markets did find some relief on Tuesday after sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu within hours, albeit at reduced volumes.

The pipeline, Saudi Arabia’s main export route bypassing wartime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, had been shut after attacks this month that Riyadh blamed on Iranian-backed groups in Iraq. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sri Lanka Easter bombings: 15 sentenced to hundreds of years in prison each over deadly terror attacks
articles.summary:
Islamic State-inspired bombings of churches and hotels in 2019 was one of the country’s worst ever attacks

A court in Sri Lanka has convicted 15 men over their involvement in the

blocks.text: A court in Sri Lanka has convicted 15 men over their involvement in the 2019 Easter bombings that killed 267 people, and sentenced them each to at least 200 years in prison, meaning they will spend the rest of their lives behind bars.

Nearly 600 people were wounded in the suicide bomb attacks on 21 April that targeted three churches and three hotels across the country during Easter services and celebrations. The bombings, which were inspired by the Islamic State (IS) group, were among the deadliest attacks in Sri Lanka’s history.
The verdict was delivered on Tuesday by a three-judge high court panel after a trial that spanned nearly five years, and amid tight security, with hundreds of police deployed around the courthouse.
The judges also ordered the property of the defendants, who were all from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community, to be confiscated.

In 2021, authorities filed 23,270 charges against 25 suspects whom they accused of planning or inspiring the attacks. The charges included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism, and firearms and explosives offences under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
None of those believed to have directly participated in the attacks are alive. Two Sri Lanka-based Islamist militant groups were accused of carrying out the bombings.
In the courtroom, the accused appeared relaxed, chatting and laughing with each other during breaks. They asked for and were granted a prayer break during the lengthy reading of the judgment.

Nine defendants were freed after the court found that the charges against them were not proven. One other died before their case reached trial. Those freed tearfully hugged the rest as they were separated from those convicted, who were later invited to argue for lenient sentences.

blocks.caption: Security personnel inspect St Sebastian’s church in Negombo on 22 April 2019, a day after the church was hit in series of bomb blasts targeting churches and luxury hotels in Sri Lanka.   Photograph: Ishara S Kodikara/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In total, five defendants were sentenced to 200 years each, five to 220 years, four to 240 years each and one to 260 years, based on their involvement in conspiring and aiding the attacks.

“What I did or didn’t do only God and I know,” said Mohamed Ibrahim Saadiq Abdulla, who was given 240 years in prison with hard labour. “In the end all people will be resurrected and God will judge everyone.”

In calculating the sentences, the court considered all seven blasts: three at churches, three at tourist hotels and one at a motel where an attacker killed himself and two others after aborting his plan to attack a fourth hotel.

Haripriya Jayasundara, who led the prosecution, called for longer prison terms, saying the defendants were part of a well-planned attack carried out with the intention of killing Christian worshippers and tourists, which was proven by a video recording left behind by one of the suicide bombers.

The video, recorded the day before the bombings, showed the attackers with their faces covered, armed with rifles and swords and pledging allegiance to the then IS leader Abu Bakhr al-Baghdadi to make Sri Lanka an Islamic nation and wage war towards that end.

Sri Lanka’s Catholic church has claimed, without providing evidence, that those identified so far as perpetrators are not the masterminds behind the bombings, and that there was a bigger conspiracy behind the attacks.
A parliamentary committee found that police and intelligence officials failed to act on repeated intelligence warnings of the attacks.
In July, a former police chief and a former senior defence ministry official were also sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks.
Sri Lanka has not carried out an execution since 1976, meaning death sentences typically result in life imprisonment.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte's defense team asks ICC to reject witness testimony
articles.summary: The defense team of former President Rodrigo Duterte has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber to reject the prosecution's request to admit the previously recorded testimony of a…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 8:42am

The defense team of former President Rodrigo Duterte has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber to reject the prosecution's request to admit the previously recorded testimony of a witness.
In a filing dated September 22, Duterte's defense team pointed out that the testimony of witness P-1100 is neither sufficiently relevant nor probative to the case.

“For the foregoing reasons, the Defence respectfully requests that the Trial Chamber REJECT the Prosecution’s Application on the basis that P-1100’s proposed evidence is not sufficiently relevant or probative of the matters in dispute in this case,” it said.

In the alternative, the Defense has requested for the ICC Trial Chamber to “REJECT the request for admission of PHL-OTP-00001799, PHL-OTP-00001796, PHL-OTP-00001794, and PHL-OTP-00001795 under Rule 68(3).”
The Defense argued that P-1100, the prosecution’s intended fact witness, does not have sufficient personal knowledge of the matters being disputed in Duterte's case.
Duterte’s lawyers argued that P-1100 cannot provide direct evidence about several matters because he allegedly has no personal knowledge of them.
The Prosecution earlier said P-1100's evidence could help establish an alleged policy to "neutralise" criminals through violent crimes, including murder.

Also, the Prosecution said the testimony could provide evidence concerning the alleged modus operandi of the Davao Death Squad and Duterte's alleged individual criminal responsibility, including his knowledge and intent.

But the Defense questioned the witness' ability to connect events that occurred before the charged period to alleged killings during Duterte's presidency. The charged period in the case runs from November 1, 2011 to March 16, 2019.
Duterte’s defense team cited portions of P-1100's statement that allegedly link killings in 2009 to killings allegedly committed in 2016.
The Defense also disputed the witness' ability to testify about the alleged structure, operations, hierarchy, or command of the DDS based on his account.
Duterte’s defense team also objected to some pieces of "associated material" that the Prosecution wants admitted together with P-1100's prior recorded testimony.
The Defense argued that simply referring to documents does not establish that the witness had "used and explained" them sufficiently for the documents to form an integral part of his testimony.
Duterte was arrested by Philippine authorities in Pasay City and was handed over to the ICC on March 11, 2025.

He was flown via a chartered plane to The Hague, where he will be tried for crimes against humanity in relation to his bloody war on drugs while he was mayor of Davao City and President of the Philippines.
The trial is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Texas camp where 27 girls died in 2025 flood investigated for manslaughter, negligent homicide
articles.summary: Camp Mystic faces a criminal investigation that could include manslaughter or negligent homicide charges in the deaths of 27 girls amid devastating flooding in Texas last year, court documents show.

image.caption: A memorial for the victims of the 2025 Camp Mystic flood in Hunt, Texas. The camp is is under criminal investigation which could lead to charges of manslaughter or negligent homicide. (Joel Angel Juarez/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Camp Mystic faces a criminal investigation that could include manslaughter or negligent homicide charges in the deaths of 27 girls amid devastating flooding in Texas last year, court documents show.
Affidavit suggests Camp Mystic had inadequate emergency plans and training

In applications for search warrants executed last week, investigators sought to obtain the electronic communications of the camp's owners, saying they could provide evidence of manslaughter, negligent homicide, child abandonment or other crimes. No charges have been brought, and a representative of the camp did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

Brant Johnston with the Texas Rangers wrote in an affidavit that Camp Mystic had inadequate emergency plans, failed to conduct emergency drills or training, and in some cabins did not have enough adult counsellors. Its owners neglected to take precautions by relocating children from low-lying cabins despite having monitored late-night flood warnings, Johnston wrote.

"Young campers cannot reasonably be expected to independently recognize a rapidly developing, life-threatening hazard or to organize and execute an evacuation absent direction from an adequate number of adult supervisors," Johnston wrote.
He concluded: "Camp Mystic, LLC was aware of and consciously disregarded a substantial and unjustifiable risk of death to the campers in their care."
Texas flash flood: Why Camp Mystic was so vulnerable

Twenty-five campers and two teenage counsellors at the Christian all-girls camp were killed as the raging Guadalupe River surged beyond its banks before dawn on July 4, 2025. Camp Mystic owner Richard Eastland also died in the flood.

For decades, Camp Mystic was a summer staple and an institution for generations of families, who dropped off their girls at the sleepaway camp to ride horses, canoe, fish and attend Bible studies. The camp did not reopen this year, and it has filed for bankruptcy reorganization.
All told, the destructive flooding killed at least 136 people along a several-kilometre stretch of the river, raising questions about how things went so terribly wrong.
Attorneys for some of the victims' families welcomed the search warrants but said they should not have been necessary.

"For more than a year, families of the 27 angels killed at Camp Mystic have fought, begged, and pleaded with the Eastland family for accountability and answers," Christina Yarnell and Brad Beckworth, attorneys for the family of victim Cile Steward, said in a written statement.
"Instead, the Eastlands have held hostage the information and answers owed to parents who deserve, more than anyone, to know the details surrounding their daughters' final moments."
Steward's body still has not been found.

Johnston wrote in the warrant that he made several visits to Camp Mystic and that he and other investigators have conducted interviews with witnesses, flood victims and people associated with the camp. But several people, including members of the Eastland family and other top camp officials, refused interviews, Johnston wrote.

The Eastland family and other camp leaders have testified in courtrooms and in front of the state legislature in the months since the flood, however, with camp director Edward Eastland offering a tearful apology.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] The P33-million question: Tracing the Duterte wealth trail
articles.summary: If Sara Duterte's wealth is clean, the ledgers will logically align. If they do not, the untouchable facade will crumble under the weight of her own financial trail.

blocks.text: If Sara Duterte's wealth is clean, the ledgers will logically align. If they do not, the untouchable facade will crumble under the weight of her own financial trail.

items: Vice President Sara Duterte's net worth reportedly increased to P98.66 million in 2025, raising questions about the sources of this wealth given her declared zero cash on hand since 2019.

Prosecutors are investigating corporate records linked to Duterte and her husband, revealing that many companies associated with them declared zero dividends, complicating the narrative of lawful income.
Duterte's involvement with GenCorp Industries and Metro City Chow raises constitutional concerns, as she has not officially divested from these businesses, potentially violating Philippine law.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Sara Duterte’s declared net worth reportedly reached P98 million in 2025, up P33 million since she became Vice President. SEC testimony before Congress and P33.26 million in Davao City contracts now give prosecutors a money trail worth pursuing.
For years, the Duterte name has carried an aura of untouchability in Philippine politics. But in the ongoing Senate impeachment trial, that aura is colliding with cold, hard corporate ledgers.

Vice President Sara Duterte’s declared net worth reached P98.66 million in 2025. That is a significant leap from the P65.04 million she declared in 2021, her final full year before assuming the vice-presidency.

This raises a fundamental question of accountability: what lawful income fueled this P33-plus million growth? Compounding the mystery is a glaring anomaly revealed by prosecutors during the trial: Duterte has declared absolutely zero cash on hand or in the bank since 2019. How does a public official’s net worth balloon by tens of millions without a single peso in the bank?

The prosecution’s search for answers hinges on the corporate records authenticated by Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Director Gerardo del Rosario. Out of 18 companies linked to Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, SEC records show 10 declared no dividends.

To understand why this is a massive red flag, we need to view a corporation as a locked vault. Even if a business makes hundreds of millions in sales, that money belongs exclusively to the company, not to the owners’ personal pockets.
The primary, legal key to open that vault and move profits to shareholders is a “dividend”. When a company declares zero dividends, that front door is shut tight.

There is nothing inherently illegal about zero dividends; businesses routinely retain earnings to reinvest or pay debts. However, if these companies are supposedly the engine behind the couple’s surging personal wealth, how did the money legally escape the corporate vault?

If dividends weren’t used, the money must have flowed through alternative routes like salaries, directors’ fees, advances, or asset sales. Every single one of these alternative routes is required by law to leave a taxable paper trail in company books and personal Statements of Assets Liabilities and Net worth (SALNs). Zero dividends do not automatically prove corruption, but they eliminate the most innocent explanation for how a politician got richer, leaving investigators to demand: show us the receipts.

blocks.caption: SALN. Vice President Sara Duterte’s SALN lists Gencorp Industries Inc., as one of the companies she has had ‘business interests and financial connections’ with since 2013.

blocks.text: GenCorp Industries perfectly illustrates the prosecution’s strongest angle. Duterte listed GenCorp as a business interest in her recent SALNs, yet her name does not appear anywhere in its SEC incorporation papers or General Information Sheets (GIS).

During Monday’s, September 21 trial, the SEC witness revealed a vital missing link: a man named Jaime T. Cruz. Cruz represents the largest subscriber in GenCorp, and he just so happens to be the biggest shareholder alongside Duterte in another company, Metro City Chow Foods Corp.

blocks.caption: Who is Jaime T. Cruz, Sara Duterte’s business partner?

blocks.text: Between 2021 and 2024, GenCorp booked a staggering P1.04 billion in sales, but netted only P8 million. Crucially, the SEC confirmed GenCorp had unrestricted retained earnings available—meaning it had the money to legally pay dividends—yet it paid out zero. Massive revenue yielded virtually no official shareholder payout.

This makes GenCorp’s government contracts highly suspicious. Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte confirmed that GenCorp secured 19 contracts from his city government starting in 2022, totaling P33.26 million.

Only four were publicly auctioned, with the rest passing through alternative small-value procurement. The mayor claimed ignorance of his sister’s ties to the firm, noting her name wasn’t on the procurement documents. But that defense highlights the contradiction: the Vice President swore to the public she had an interest in the firm, while hiding her name from the SEC and the city that paid it millions.

Then there is Metro City Chow, which introduces a severe constitutional problem. The Philippine Constitution strictly prohibits the Vice President from participating, directly or indirectly, in any business.

SEC records list Duterte as a continuing director and compensation committee member of Metro City Chow through 2025—three full years into her term. Furthermore, the SEC testified this week that Duterte has failed to transfer ownership of her business interests in all but two corporations. There is no deed of sale or divestment on file for Metro City Chow.

While the defense might attempt to write this off as a clerical oversight, four years of official corporate filings cannot be casually brushed aside, especially for the second-highest official in the land.

blocks.caption: Jollibee enters the menu as impeach court scrutinizes Sara Duterte businesses

blocks.text: Public officials who project an image of invincibility often stumble not on grand conspiracies, but on basic accounting.

Prosecutors must not overreach by claiming all corporate revenues are Duterte’s personal wealth. But they now have the framework of a devastating case: unexplained wealth growth, zero cash in the bank, millions in un-bidded city contracts awarded to a firm she claims but doesn’t officially own, and clear evidence she failed to divest from private business as required by the Constitution.
If her wealth is clean, the ledgers will logically align. If they do not, the untouchable facade will crumble under the weight of her own financial trail. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Nov. 16-18 set as non-working days in Metro Manila for ASEAN Summit
articles.summary: Malacañang has declared November 16 to 18, 2026 as special non-working days in the National Capital Region as the Philippines hosts the 49th ASEAN Summit and related summits.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 8:17am

(L-R) Myanmar's Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs U Hau Khan Sum, Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, East Timor's Prime Minister Xanana Gusmao, Vietnam's Prime Minister Le Minh Hung, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, Brunei's Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto, Cambodia's Prime Minister Hun Manet and Laos’ Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone pose for a group photo during the opening ceremony of the 48th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Cebu, central Philippines on May 8, 2026.
AFP / Aaron Favila / pool
MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang has declared November 16 to 18, 2026 as special non-working days in the National Capital Region as the Philippines hosts the 49th ASEAN Summit and related summits.

Acting Executive Secretary Ralph Recto signed the proclamation on September 17, declaring the three-day holiday to help ease traffic congestion and ensure the safety and security of summit participants.
ASEAN leaders and other world leaders are expected to attend the summits, although the participation of United States President Donald Trump remains unconfirmed.
The special non-working days will cover Monday, November 16, through Wednesday, November 18.
The proclamation cited the need to alleviate vehicular traffic in Metro Manila and allow authorities to ensure the safety and security of participants during the high-level meetings.
The Philippines is set to host the ASEAN Summit and related meetings in November, bringing together leaders and senior officials from ASEAN member states and dialogue partners.
The ASEAN-related meetings scheduled in Metro Manila include the 16th ASEAN Maritime Forum on November 17 and the 14th Expanded ASEAN Maritime Forum on November 18.

articles.title: Review urged after blood-spattered shirt ads ran alongside domestic violence news in Australia
articles.summary: Gruesome ads embedded in articles about family violence ‘make light’ of violence and could distress victim-survivors, expert warns

blocks.text: News stories about domestic violence inadvertently ran alongside advertisements for faux-bloodstained shirts reading “problem solved”, prompting advocates for victim-survivors to urge publishers to avoid making light of recent deaths.

Australia is reckoning with a surge in family and domestic violence incidents after three women were allegedly murdered in unrelated incidents on Saturday, and police allege a mother stabbed her three children on Sunday.
On Sunday articles about the incidents were published on a number of Australian news websites, where readers were confronted by a gruesome advertisement for the blood-soaked costume shirts.

The shirts are sold under titles containing the words “bloody” and “halloween” by online clothing retailer Menweary. Similar products are listed as Halloween outfits on Amazon, Etsy and other larger retailers.
Denise Buiten, an expert in media and gendered violence, said the ad placement created an inappropriate contrast with the subjects of the articles.

“When you put in that context, it’s more than just tasteless humour, it becomes something else, gives a very different meaning to the story on that page,” said Buiten, a senior lecturer in sociology and social justice at the University of Notre Dame Australia.
“It strips a lot of the dignity away.”
Patty Kinnersly, chief executive of advocacy group Our Watch, said the unexpected ads in the article could distress victim-survivors and “make light” of the violence they have faced.

“We know that one of the key drivers of violence against women is the condoning of violence, [including] messages that excuse violence, make light of it, or present it as normal or acceptable,” Kinnersly said.
Kinnersly said media outlets and advertisers needed to review the incident and implement stronger measures to protect consumers from potentially harmful advertising mismatches.

The Guardian has technical protocols to block harmful advertising but was among the outlets to feature the ad. A spokesperson said the ad breached Guardian advertising guidelines and was taken down after the organisation was made aware of the ad.
The Sydney Morning Herald’s parent company, Nine, attributed its publication of the ad to the Google-run distributor, AdSense.
“AdSense is responsible for screening these type of ads before they go live,” a Nine spokesperson said. “Once our teams were alerted to the content, we removed and blocked the advertiser.”
News.com.au’s editor, Kerry Warren, said parent company News Corp was working with the third-party provider to ensure the “error” did not happen again.
“Once brought to our attention we removed it as quickly as possible,” Warren said. “We apologise for any distress caused.”
after newsletter promotion
‘Slipped through a crack’
While websites can sell their own advertising space, some give Google power to allocate ads in real time from an international open market, linking millions of advertisers with millions of sites.

A Google spokesperson said the company reviewed ads under its policies and allowed publishers to impose further limits if they wished, by blocking specific sources, advertisers, websites or categories.

Christopher Brown, from the University of New South Wales’s Australian Graduate School of Management, said ads carry content tags but clothing-tagged ads would not have been caught by screening measures.
“It’s slipped through a crack,” Brown said.
Advertisers could also try to target their ads to automatically appear in articles with related content. Brown said content-targeting software, if used in this case, could have miscalculated.
The incident suggested that bad actors could potentially use mass digital advertising systems to distribute potentially harmful content without being flagged, Brown said.
Menweary and its owner were contacted for comment.

In 2017, Google’s ad systems plastered ads from governments and major companies, from Pepsi to the Guardian, across extremist content on YouTube, leading to the loss of millions of dollars of advertising contracts.

The “problem solved” shirt design attracted controversy in 2025 when worn by school teachers in Arizona, US, weeks after the fatal shooting of political activist Charlie Kirk. The choice of the shirts was reportedly unrelated to Kirk’s death.

“Although these shirts can be purchased on Amazon, they celebrate real-life murder, and are, minimally, extremely short-sighted and tone deaf,” Republican state representative, Rachel Keshel, said at the time.

articles.title: Indigenous leaders call for change in Sask. health care after woman's death during childbirth
articles.summary: First Nations leaders say a declining health-care system and systemic racism within that system both contributed to Chelsea Bear's death from complications during the birth of her twins last month in…

image.caption: Deb Bear, left, speaks about the death of her daughter Chelsea Bear, pictured on right. She was accompanied by her niece Amanda Bear, centre, and leaders from Flying Dust First Nation and the Meadow Lake Tribal Council at a news conference Tuesday in Saskatoon. (CBC News)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New

First Nations leaders say a declining health-care system and systemic racism within that system both contributed to Chelsea Bear's death from complications during the birth of her twins last month in Saskatoon.
Chelsea Bear's family says she was sent home from hospital without proper care
WARNING: This story contains details about death in childbirth.
First Nations leaders say a declining health-care system and systemic racism within that system both contributed to a mother's death from complications during the birth of her twins.

"No matter where you are in life, you should have fair and equitable treatment. Everybody should be treated the same," Meadow Lake Tribal Council vice-chief Richard Derocher said on Tuesday, speaking alongside the family of Chelsea Bear at a news conference in Saskatoon.

Bear, a member of Flying Dust First Nation, went to hospital on Aug. 10 in Meadow Lake, in pain and bleeding, but was sent home without receiving proper care, her family said. She was 36 weeks pregnant and her pregnancy was considered high-risk.

The next day, the pain and bleeding increased severely, and Bear returned to the hospital. She was ultimately taken to Saskatoon, where the first twin was delivered stillborn and the second baby was born very weak, her family said.

Bear died after their deliveries, in the early hours of Aug. 12. She was 36 years old and left behind four other children, in addition to the surviving twin, Gracie, who is still in the neonatal intensive care unit in Saskatoon.
Her family said she died from hemorrhaging blood due to placental abruption — which is when the placenta separates too early from the uterus.
They said that if Bear would have received proper care when she first went to hospital, she and both her babies would still be alive.
"She must have been so scared, I was thinking, just losing all the blood.… It must have hurt her," Chelsea's mother Deb Bear said at a news conference Tuesday in Saskatoon.
"I just don't want this ever to happen to anybody else."
Bear's family is the second Indigenous family to speak out and call for change after the death of a mother during childbirth in Saskatchewan this year.

items: Family seeks answers after Indigenous mother dies in delivery room at Saskatoon hospital

blocks.text: Jaali Sutherland-Weenie, from Beardy's & Okemasis Cree Nation, died on April 26 after first going to the hospital in Rosthern with severe back pain and vomiting, then being sent to Saskatoon. Her family said she was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, a blood pressure condition. Her baby girl survived.
Sutherland-Weenie's family said they believed she would have been treated differently if she were not Indigenous.
Systemic racism alleged

On Tuesday, near the end of a lengthy news conference, Derocher said that speaking about Bear's death is complicated "because of all the things that are not being said" when people are "trying to be as nice as possible."

He and Meadow Lake Tribal Council Tribal Chief Jeremy Norman both said they were on a conference call with representatives of the Saskatchewan Health Authority that took place after MLTC reached out to them about Bear's death.
They said they expressed frustration that they weren't getting answers and told the SHA they were considering holding a news conference.
Norman said an SHA representative "basically told us, keep quiet, because it's so hard to get doctors in our region, it's so hard to get people to come and work in the north."

Derocher said those words "burnt me hard," and are another example of the systemic racism that happens every day, when First Nations people are asked "to keep silent, do not speak of this issue, do not bring it forth."

He and the other chiefs also spoke about how they have seen the quality of health care declining for everyone in Saskatchewan over the past two decades — in everything from hospital care to long-term care — and how they want to work with the province to make positive changes.
SHA to conduct patient safety review
The SHA declined an interview request, but issued a statement extending their condolences to the family and community for the "profound and tragic loss."

The statement didn't directly answer a question about Norman and Derocher's account of the conference call where they said they were asked to keep quiet. The statement said the SHA met with the MLTC to hear their concerns, but at the time of the meeting, "the SHA had not received consent from the family to discuss the specifics of their case with MLTC."
"We have since received the family's consent and will continue our discussions with MLTC in the coming days," the SHA's statement said.

items: Nurses' union sounds alarm on short-staffing, lack of resources in Sask. maternity wards

blocks.text: The health authority said it would be conducting a thorough patient safety review.

"The SHA acknowledges the complex and dynamic conditions that our maternal health and obstetrical clinical teams operate within, and appreciate their commitment, clinical expertise and professionalism."
Independent investigation called for
The MLTC chiefs and Flying Dust First Nation Chief Tyson Bear are calling for more than a patient safety review.
"We are calling for a thorough, independent, transparent investigation, so Chelsea's family can get the answers they deserve," Chief Bear said.
Chelsea Bear's death was not an isolated incident in the health-care system, the chiefs said.
In a news release, they highlighted that it is the sixth quality-of-care incident that the Meadow Lake Tribal Council has tried to raise with the SHA this year.
"We're here for a better health system. We're here to make change," Tribal Chief Norman said.
"It's unfortunate things like this have to happen before we look at making change, before we really dig in to say, 'What's the problem?'"
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Hannah Spray works as a reporter and copy editor. She began her journalism career in newspapers, first in her hometown of Meadow Lake, Sask., moving on to Fort St. John, B.C., and then to the Saskatoon StarPhoenix. She joined CBC in 2022. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to HannahSpray.10

articles.title: Hamilton-born NHL prospect collapsed after coaches didn't submit workout for review: university
articles.summary: Hockey coaches at Arizona State University didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before an outdoor workout on a hot August day that saw Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapse,…

image.caption: Hamilton-born Matthew Mayich, who was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues in 2023, was at an early-morning outdoor workout with the Arizona State University hockey team on Aug. 20 when he collapsed. (St. Louis Blues)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Hockey coaches at Arizona State University didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before an outdoor workout on a hot August day that saw Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapse, leaving him in hospital in critical condition, says a review by the Tempe-based school.
Lawyer says Hamilton-born St. Louis draft pick in stable, critical condition, family 'praying for a miracle'

Hockey coaches at Arizona State University (ASU) didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before an outdoor workout last month that saw NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapse, leaving him in hospital in critical condition.

James Rund, the university official leading the review, wrote that the Hamilton-born 21-year-old collapsed just before 8:30 a.m. during the Aug. 20 training session at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus.

The report, which calls for a "a blue-ribbon advisory panel," said the temperature was about 30 C, and the student athletes were involved in "calisthenics, bodyweight exercises such as pushups and planks, and running."

items: Parents of NHL prospect hospitalized after collapse at team workout say he's a 'fighter'

blocks.text: The hockey coaches asked permission for Timothy Zeisel, who was there for the workout and had "spoken with the ASU Hockey team in the 2025-26 season about topics of leadership and teamwork," to speak to the team. However, the coaches didn't "submit a plan of training activities for review by ASU’s strength and conditioning coaches" before training began.

Near the end of the workout, "Matthew appeared to struggle, and then in rapid succession stumbled, dropped the medicine ball and fell to the ground. He attempted to get up and resume running but fell to his knees," wrote Rund, ASU's senior vice-president of educational outreach and student services.
Mayich in stable, critical condition, lawyer says

The Mayich family's lawyer, Rob Carey, said on Tuesday that "Matthew is in stable but critical condition still. The family is still praying for a miracle, but nothing has significantly changed. But even if that happens, we will never have the young man who came to Arizona last month, a hockey star and (by all accounts) a wonderful person."
In an interview last week from Phoenix, Ariz., with CBC News, Mayich's father, John Mayich, said "we know Matthew's a fighter and we're hoping he pulls through this."
Before the workout, Matthew was "perfectly healthy," said his mother, Christina.
Carey said that "when Matthew went down, there was no plan and no preparation, so he was treated in a way that hurt his chances rather than helped them."
"A month later, nobody's been named, nobody's been suspended, nobody's been fired for violating the very policies ASU published today, and the university wants to appoint a committee."

He added that "a committee isn't going to tell us why grown men with a rulebook in their hands let this happen to a young man at his first real workout in the desert. That's what an investigation is for, and it's why we're going to ask the county attorney to do one."
Carey said in early September that based on his own investigation, he believes Mayich endured a "military-style, brutal, gruelling workout" with no breaks and no water for over an hour.

"You have an elite NHL-drafted athlete showing up on the first coach-led workout, the very first day the team could organize formally, and he left the field with no chance of recovery," Carey said. "Obviously there's something wrong."

Rund said ASU would "be undertaking a comprehensive review of its practices to identify and implement best practices regarding the planning, conduct and monitoring of athletic activities. and the response to emergencies that arise during athletic activities."
In early September, a spokesperson for the ASU Police Department said they were investigating what happened to Mayich, which is a "standard procedure" for an incident of this severity.
The report said ASU would have a panel of experts provide best practice recommendations for:

items: Planning and approval of outdoor athletic activities, including strength and conditioning activities, practices and competitions.
Staffing, monitoring and conduct of outdoor athletic activities, including adjustments to address changed conditions or adverse reactions.
Preparation for and response to adverse events or reactions occurring during outdoor athletic activities.
Use of outside consultants in the planning and delivery of strength and conditioning, and practice activities.

blocks.text: Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020. He was selected in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft by the St. Louis Blues.

Doug Armstrong, the Blues' president of hockey operations, said in a news release in late August, "The entire Blues organization is keeping Matthew Mayich close to our hearts as we pray for his comfort and recovery while he continues to undergo medical treatment in Arizona."
The organization also extends its "deepest support" to his family, friends and teammates during this difficult time, Armstrong said.
'A tremendous hockey player'

During his six seasons with the Huskies and one as a member of the Hamilton Jr. Bulldogs, Mayich established "himself as a tremendous hockey player and, more importantly, an outstanding person both on and off the ice," the Hamilton Steel Hockey Club, formerly the Huskies, said.

The statement was sent to CBC Hamilton on behalf of the organization, former Huskies president Mike Spadafora and former Huskies head coach Chris Travale. Spadafora is currently the councillor for Hamilton's Ward 14 and running for re-election in the Oct. 26 municipal vote.

"Without fail, whenever [Mayich] is asked, he comes back every year to speak and skate with a new crop of young kids," Travale said. "His message is always about so much more than hockey — it’s about relationships, friendships, and the experiences you have along the hockey journey."

items: Hamilton NHL prospect Matthew Mayich 'needs a miracle' after training collapse, family lawyer says

blocks.text: Mayich's father said Matthew "didn't care if he was at a small rink in Hamilton or a big rink in St. Louis with a lot of people — he just loves the game."
The incident has made waves in the sports world, prompting the Professional Hockey Players’ Association to speak up about the lack of protections for young athletes.

"When athletes feel pressure to remain silent about an injury, illness, exhaustion or concern because they fear the consequences of speaking up, the system has failed them," said PHPA executive director Brian Ramsay in a statement on Sept. 10 that doesn't directly name Mayich.
"Athletes should never have to choose between their health and their careers. Period."

articles.title: Trump signs 'tremendous' Greenland security deal
articles.summary: Donald Trump strikes a security deal with Greenland and Denmark on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The deal comes after Trump repeatedly said the US should own the Danish territory.

image.caption: Trump signed the deal after his speech at the UN General AssemblyImage: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed a security agreement with Denmark and Greenland to strengthen Arctic and North Atlantic security.
Trump, Greenland Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen signed the deal on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday.
The White House released the text of the deal shortly after that.
What's in the Greenland deal?
The deal, which the president first announced earlier this month, bolsters US military and security presence on Greenland.
The US will reestablish a military base in south Greenland in Narsarsuaq and set up the other base on the eastern coast of the island in Mestersvig.

Trump said during his speech at the United Nations General Assembly that the US would "immediately begin the process of developing a significant military presence in appropriate locations and constructing two very important military bases."
He said the deal was "tremendous" for Europe and the US just before he signed it, adding, "And for Greenland, it’s going to be incredible."
Under the agreement, the US will be "allowed to modernize and expand its activities" at the Space Force base.
The deal also reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Denmark and Greenland.
Trump has long said he wanted the US to take over Greenland
The agreement comes after months of pressure from Trump,who has long said he wants the US to control Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, a NATO ally.
Behind the scenes, American, Danish, and Greenlandic officials worked many months to address Trump's security concerns regarding the resource-rich island.
The dispute unsettled most Greenlanders and created tensions between the US, Denmark, and the European Union, which quickly increased security exercises and financial support for the Arctic island.
What did Trump really gain from the Greenland deal?
The race for Arctic

Greeland's future has come under the spotlight globally because of trade interests and expectations of future resource development. At least two-thirds of its territory lies within the Arctic Circle, where melting sea ice has opened new maritime routes.
Although the US played a prominent role in Greenland for decades, its military presence on the island has declined since 1945.
From having thousands of troops stationed across 17 bases and installations, only about 200 personnel remain today at Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland.
Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland's prime minister, described the agreement as "a win-win arrangement."

Last year, the Danish Parliament approved a bill allowing US military bases on Danish territory, expanding an agreement it had reached with the Biden administration in 2023. The deal granted US forces broad access to air bases in Denmark.

blocks.caption: US, Denmark and Greenland sign defense dealImage: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: Wide US mobility on Greenland

The agreement grants US military forces broad freedom of movement in Greenland and its territorial waters and restricts non-NATO countries from establishing military facilities in Greenland or maintaining a "permanent" military presence unless the signatories agree otherwise.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte welcomed the signing of the agreement, writing on X that "this agreement, together with NATO's growing role in securing this vital region, enhances our collective security and supports a safer and more stable future for all of us."

Editor's note: We join our media colleagues in objection to the White House barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico. We are not going to use photos or video material produced by the White House and distributed through its official communication channels until further notice.

articles.title: Pay rent, eat or keep warm? Growing numbers face hard choices as housing benefit gap grows
articles.summary:
Wirral mother among renters turning to food banks as gap between a two-bed and housing benefit hits £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 in London

Do you prioritise paying the rent,…

blocks.text: Do you prioritise paying the rent, putting food on the table or keeping the house warm in winter? In practice, says Laura Braddock, a single mum from Wirral, Merseyside, you always pay the rent first and improvise the rest. “If I’ve got a roof over our head, then everything else I can muddle through.”

The pressing problem for Braddock, 39, is that muddling through is getting harder. The monthly rent for her two-bedroom flat far outstrips the local housing allowance (LHA) she receives – and the gap may widen.
She pays her landlord £550 a month, but receives £425 in housing allowance, leaving her to make up a £125 “rent gap” out of her grocery and heating budgets.

The former shop worker has a range of tried and tested strategies to cope, and to shield her son as far as possible from cost of living pressures. She may pay half the gas bill. She’ll eat cheap pasta and beans – or skip her own meals altogether.
In January, however, these strategies, and the constant juggling with ever tighter budgets, failed. She was forced to go to a food bank for the first time in years to make end meet.

It’s hard, she reflects, and the stress can affect her mental health. “When I’m tired or hungry or whatever, that then has an impact on me, the way I parent. I’ve got no energy sometimes … It’s difficult.”

blocks.caption: Letting sign in London, where rent costs can outstrip housing support by as much as £324 a month. Photograph: William Barton/Alamy
Letting signs in London, where rent costs can outstrip housing support by as much as £324 a month. Photograph: Simon Dack/Alamy

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of low-income households are feeling the same pressures, said Trussell, the food bank network. Unless the government links LHA more closely to actual rents, it added, many more will be forced to turn to charity food.

The growing gap between LHA rates and local rents means more than half (62%) of private renters receiving housing support have gone without food and heating in the past six months because they could not afford them, Trussell estimated.

The gap is expected to reach record levels this autumn. According to the Resolution Foundation thinktank, the average difference between rent and LHA faced by a low-income household renting a two-bedroom home in the private sector is £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 a month in parts of London.

Trussell wants the government to relink LHA to the cheapest 30% of local rents. It estimates this would lift 105,000 people out of severe hardship by 2028-29, including 40,000 children. The Resolution Foundation estimates this would cost £2bn a year.

Campaigners will focus on the LHA gap – the consequence of years of austerity and rising private rents – in the run-up to next month’s budget, arguing it is an effective way to give low-income families “breathing space” from cost of living pressures.
after newsletter promotion

Beatrice Orchard, the head of policy at Trussell, said: “Nobody should be forced to choose between paying the rent and putting food on the table. But for increasing numbers of UK renters, this is already a bleak reality. Keeping LHA frozen while rents rise is driving people to food banks.”
Governments have often been reluctant to match rents and housing support, fearing landlords will simply put up rents, or that tenants will move to plusher rented homes.

Braddock, who fears that her landlord is preparing to put up her rent, tightening her budget even further, disagrees: “If the local housing allowance matched the going rate for a two-bedroom or a one-bedroom [place] then people don’t need to move. It’ll just mean they don’t struggle to get through the month, because the rent’s being paid.

“I don’t think the government understands … From a parent’s point of view, you’ve got to think about keeping your kids safe and your kids warm. And they wonder why there’s an epidemic of mental health [concerns]”.

A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said: “We’re tackling the impact of rising rents and the housing shortage with our commitment to build 1.5m homes – including the biggest boost to social and affordable housing in a generation.
“Local housing allowance rates are reviewed annually, and future decisions will be taken in the context of the government’s welfare priorities, and the fiscal context.”

articles.title: England’s mayors should face greater scrutiny as powers expand, thinktank says
articles.summary:
IPPR North says one bad decision could derail devolution agenda as regions gain control of billions in funding

England’s mayors should face much greater official scrutiny to avoid Andy…
articles.byline: Josh Halliday North of England editor

blocks.text: England’s mayors should face much greater official scrutiny to avoid Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda being “derailed by one bad decision”, a thinktank has said.
Ministers will set out plans next month to give regional leaders control over potentially billions of pounds of additional funding under a “transformational” shift of power outside Whitehall.

From 2028, mayors will be able to keep a share of income tax generated in their areas – giving them greater scope to borrow for major infrastructure projects – as well as retain business rates from 2027 and raise further funds through a “tourist tax”.

IPPR North, whose researchers have worked closely with Burnham’s government, welcomed the “bold and ambitious” plans as a step towards “reversing decades of damaging over-centralisation that has held the country back”.
It called for mayors to be allowed to keep a 5% share of income tax, which would move an extra £3.8bn a year out of Whitehall and roughly double the funding under their control.
However, the thinktank said increasingly powerful mayors should be subject to much tougher oversight.
In its 30-page report, IPPR North warned: “A bad decision or mismanaged funding from any one authority risks turning public opinion against devolution and undoing progress.”

Its proposals include establishing new regional audit offices to scrutinise how money is spent and what it delivers. It is also proposed that each region should be overseen by a senior accounting officer, similar to the model of permanent secretaries running government departments.

Larger mayoral authorities, such as London, Greater Manchester and the West Midlands, should be overseen by beefed-up accountability committees to guard against any “misuse of funds, corruption and elite capture by lobbying interests”, the thinktank said.

Burnham, a former Greater Manchester mayor, has placed the transfer of power outside Whitehall at the heart of his government, establishing No 10 North in Manchester to act as the engine room of rapid devolution.
Proposals outlined in a Cabinet Office paper in July, weeks after Burnham became prime minister, would represent the most dramatic shift of authority to the English regions in modern times.

There are concerns, however, about the capacity of newer and smaller combined authorities to take on these expanded powers, which include employment support, local transport, housing, innovation, local energy and cultural investment.

blocks.caption: Regional mayors at Downing Street for a devolution meeting in July 2024. Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./Alamy

blocks.text: While some mayoral authorities are well established, others, such as the Reform UK-led bodies in Hull and East Yorkshire and Greater Lincolnshire, were only founded last year. Several other planned mayoral authorities, spanning millions of people along the south coast and in north-west England, have not yet been established.
Ministers are due to set out a timeline for fiscal devolution to the English regions in a white paper to be published alongside the autumn budget on 28 October.
Aditi Sriram, the lead author of the IPPR North report, said Britain was at a “defining moment” in how it is governed and that accountability was essential to the success of devolution.

“For too long, mayors have been expected to drive growth with one hand tied behind their backs, reliant on Whitehall for the money and permission to get things done,” she said. “Critics are loud, political trust is faltering, and the public wants to see action, so the devolution agenda cannot afford to fail.”

Jim O’Neill, the former Treasury minister who advised Burnham before he became prime minister, said in a foreword to the report that critics would dismiss devolution as an “irrelevance and a probable source of wasted taxpayers’ money”.

But he said the best answer to those “cynics” would be to hand mayors of the most populated areas the greatest powers. “This is assuming they have the capacity to cope, the desire to be accountable and, of course, just like Greater Manchester has had, the aspiration to be bold,” he said.

articles.title: DILG, DepEd to formalize ‘visible patrols’ in public schools
articles.summary: These "visible patrols," according to Castro, may be composed of barangay security officers, particularly women, to monitor situations inside the schools.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 7:00am
School officials use handheld metal detectors to check students’ bags at Mayamot National High School in Antipolo, Rizal on June 29, 2026.
The Philippines STAR / Walter Bollozos

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) and the Department of Education (DepEd) are expected to formalize an agreement on deploying "visible patrols" inside public schools following a series of school shooting incidents this year.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said in a press briefing on Tuesday, September 22, that a memorandum of agreement between the two agencies is set to be released by next week regarding the proposed safety protocol.
These "visible patrols," according to Castro, may be composed of barangay security officers, particularly women, to monitor situations inside the schools.

“Sila po [DILG] ay magkakaroon ng memorandum of agreement or pagkakasundo ng DepEd tungkol sa kanilang suhestiyon na magkaroon ng mga bantay sa loob ng paaralan na maaari ay mga tanod, lalong-lalo na mga kababaihan,”
(The DILG will have a memorandum of agreement with DepEd about their suggestion to have lookouts inside the school, which could be barangay security officers, especially women.)
The proposed security officer, Castro said, is currently under review.
‘Very disturbing’ situation
Meanwhile, Castro said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has learned about the incident and directed immediate action on what he called a ‘very disturbing’ situation.
According to Castro, Marcos read the alleged letter written by the 16-year-old Grade 9 student who shot 10 of his classmates, killing three, including himself.

“So nung nabasa ng pangulo 'yung hindi umanong sulat nung nagsagawa nito, ang sabi ng Pangulo ay very disturbing at hindi ito normal na pangyayari,” Castro said. “Kakaiba siya, hindi siya ordinaryo. So kailangan talagang aksyunan.”

(So, when the president read the alleged letter of the suspect, the president said it was very disturbing and that it was not a normal event. It is unusual; it is not ordinary. So it needs to be acted upon.)

In response, aside from the proposed security protocol by the DILG and DepEd, Castro said the Department of Social Welfare and Development is currently conducting parenting services to guide families on raising children.
The DSWD is also conducting trauma-informed care to help school personnel recognize concerning behaviors among students, according to Castro.
