articles.title: 'What he’s doing is positively un-American': Late-night hosts react to Trump media ban
articles.summary: The comedians of late-night television have a vested interest in protecting the First Amendment. So when U.S. President Donald Trump announced he was banning news outlets CNN, MS NOW, and Politico…

image.caption: Late-night television comedians NBC's Seth Meyers, ABC's Jimmy Kimmel, NBC's Jimmy Fallon, and Comedy Central's Jon Stewart accused U.S. President Donald Trump of tramping on the constitutionally protected freedom of the press with his White House media ban. (NBC/ABC/NBC/Comedy Central/ YouTube)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The comedians of late-night television have a vested interest in protecting the First Amendment. So when U.S. President Donald Trump announced he was banning news outlets CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House last Friday, they came out swinging.
Comedians try to find humour in Trump's decision to bar CNN, Politico, MS NOW from White House
Jon Stewart, Seth Meyers, Jimmy Kimmel and even — to some extent — the famously "not very political" Jimmy Fallon have built their careers making fun of the U.S. president.

So when Donald Trump announced he was banning news outlets CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House last Friday, the late-night television hosts came out swinging in defence of the First Amendment, which protects freedom of speech and the press.
Were they outraged? Definitely. Were they funny? You be judge.
"The White House press pool is more of a mess than the reflecting pool right now," said Jimmy Kimmel, whose jokes have landed him in trouble with the Trump administration before.
"What he's doing is positively un-American," he said on ABC's Jimmy Kimmel Live!

"The five networks, including Fox, joined forces to put out a statement saying the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.... Do you realize how far south somebody has to go for Fox News to defend CNN?" he added.
Helipad event offers fodder for jokes

Both Kimmel and NBC host Seth Meyers pointed out how Trump's media ban appeared to backfire when the White House press pool, which usually has eyes on the president at all official events, refused to cover his opening of a new helicopter landing pad.

There were visuals of the ribbon cutting from the White House's own video stream, but there was no microphone there to pick up what the president was saying. All that could be heard was the whirring of the helicopter blades.
"The best is, that sound is always the substance of what Trump is saying," said Meyers.

Yesterday, the Trump administration released a statement reiterating its position that, "White House access is a privilege — not a right" and rejecting claims the media ban undermined reporters' First Amendment rights.
That argument was put to Trump directly by some of the journalists remaining in the White House.
Acting like a diva
Meyers played a clip of Trump's response, saying the president "sounds like an aging Hollywood starlet chewing out a director for cutting her line."
Jimmy Fallon compared him to the host of The Traitors. "He even dressed like Alan Cumming to tell them, 'You're banished from my castle.'"

He also suggested the First Lady wished she, too, would be banished to get away from her husband. "In a related story, Melania just applied to be a reporter for CNN, MSN NOW and Politico," joked Fallon.
On The Daily Show, Jon Stewart focused on Trump's reason for the media ban: his disappointment in the outlets' negative news stories.
Outrage and incredulity

"Have you tried president-ing better?" asked Stewart. "I mean give the press something to work with. Oh, here's a positive story: I never thought my car could take $140 worth of gas in such a small tank!"
Stewart toggled between outrage and incredulity as he replayed footage of Trump justifying his media ban.
"Not for nothing, have we ever had a president just flat out in the Oval Office come out against the Constitution?"
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Cyclist who dressed as man to avoid Taliban wins silver medal

"I always dressed as a man to go to training, wearing two or three different masks so ‌people ⁠would not recognise or attack me," Hashimi previously told Reuters., external

Hashimi now lives and trains in Italy thanks to help from the Italian former world champion Alessandra Cappellotto.
Looking back at life in Afghanistan, Hashimi said the Taliban "took away our freedom".
"This silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women, and I'm really happy," she said.
"I'm not alone, I know that behind me millions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me."
Hashimi and her sister competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics and are now setting their sights on the 2028 Los Angeles Games.
"I never want to give up," Hashimi said, "and hopefully we can see [what can happen] again in Los Angeles."

articles.title: Top South African policeman charged with sexual offences
articles.summary: Shadrack Sibiya, who has made no comment, is alleged to have groomed a 16-year-old and raped an 18-year-old.

blocks.text: One of South Africa's highest ranking police officers has been charged with sexual offences at a brief appearance at a court north-west of Johannesburg.

The charges relate to allegations that Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He is also facing a charge of trafficking, which could mean that others may be arrested in relation to this case.
The suspended deputy police commissioner, who was detained on Monday, has made no comment.
The 59-year-old is due to appear in court again on 29 September for a bail application. Prosecutors are expected to oppose bail.
The state has also requested that the court change the prison where Sibiya will be held in the meantime as there are indications of a potential escape plan, national broadcaster SABC is reporting.
The case comes as the police service is in the spotlight at a major public inquiry over allegations of corruption and collusion with criminals.

The inquiry, known as the Madlanga Commission, began last September and has heard accusations that Sibiya received a gift of 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract.
He denied the allegation.

articles.title: High fuel prices force bus operators to cut trips, seek fare hike
articles.summary: Amid the incessant fuel price hikes, several bus operators have been forced to reduce their number of trips to avoid operating at a loss.

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 12:42am
Amid the incessant fuel price hikes, several bus operators have been forced to reduce their number of trips to avoid operating at a loss.

In a “24 Oras” report by Oscar Oida on Tuesday, Alex Yague, director of the Provincial Bus Operators Association of the Philippines (PBOAP), shared that several bus terminals now have fewer buses dispatched for trips.
“Lahat ng mga operator ngayon, nagbabawas na ng biyahe,” Yague said.
(All operators right now are reducing their trips.)
“Actually, makikita mo sa mga terminal nila, ‘pag pumasok sa terminal ng bus, napakaraming bus na nakaparada doon na walang biyahe,” he added.
(Actually, you can see it in their terminals—when you go inside a bus terminal, there are so many buses parked there with no scheduled trips.)
To cushion the impact of the recent fuel price hike, PBOAP urged the government to approve the proposed fare increase, stating it would sustain their livelihoods far better than government subsidies.
In March, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. suspended the scheduled implementation of the fare hike, noting that it would pose a heavy burden on commuters.
“Nakikita namin na dapat nang i-lift na ‘yung suspension [at] ma-implement na ‘yung fare increase para magpatuloy ang serbisyo ng mga provincial buses sa publiko,” Yague said.
(We believe it is time to lift the suspension and implement the fare increase so provincial buses can continue serving the public.)
Charlie Portizo, a 50-year-old jeepney driver, echoed the same call for a fare increase.
Portizo said that while he works hard every day, he takes home very little income for his family.
“Minsan nakaka-P500 pa rin, ‘yun naman ‘yung pinakamalaki pero minsan wala na. ‘Yung diesel namin ‘yung P800 doon na napupunta ‘yung kita namin—sa diesel na lang talaga,” Portiza said.
(Sometimes I still make P500—that’s the highest—but other times, I take home nothing. Around P800 goes toward our diesel—our earnings really just end up going to fuel.)
“Sa totoo lang, sir, ‘di naman namin kailangan talaga ng ayuda. Kailangan namin ngayon, sir, ‘yung taasan man lang ‘yung pamasahe kahit ‘yun man lang. Para kahit papaano maka-survive kami,” he added.
(To be honest, sir, we don't really need subsidies. What we need right now, sir, is at least a fare increase—even just that. So that somehow, we can survive.)
‘Last resort’
The implementation of a fare increase remains the government’s last resort, according to Department of Transportation (DOTr) Secretary Banoy Lopez.
“Sana ho, ang pag-i-impose natin ng fare hike ay maging last resort,” Lopez said.
(Hopefully, imposing a fare hike will be our last resort.)
“‘Pag nagtaas po tayo ng pamasahe, sigurado po makakadagdag din ‘yan sa magiging inflation. Makakadagdag sa presyo rin po ng serbisyo at sa presyo ng mga goods,” he added.
(If we raise fares, it will certainly contribute to inflation. It will also add to the prices of services and basic goods.)
The DOTr added that the government is doing everything it can to assist drivers and operators.

Lopez has ordered the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board to study the situation and submit recommendations regarding the possibility of a fare hike. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: 'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
articles.summary: The BBC goes inside the prison where prisoners were trapped in stifling, cramped conditions.

blocks.text: Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.
The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.
Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.
The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.
Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation.
"I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.

When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin.
The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window.

"One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.
Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.
The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.
Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.
The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.

As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.
He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe.
"People were calling for help, some were already very weak."
But no-one came to help, he and others allege.
"While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency.
"We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door.
"We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."
Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.

The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye.
"The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.

articles.title: Skirts take star billing as Prada eschews trousers and dresses in Milan
articles.summary:
Combination of Miuccia Prada with Belgian designer Raf Simons once again spins gold for fashion house

Miuccia Prada’s style formula is simple: begin with a great skirt. Her personal uniform…

blocks.text: Miuccia Prada’s style formula is simple: begin with a great skirt. Her personal uniform is a knee-length skirt, A-line or pleated, most often with a plain sweater and kitten heels. The Prada collection that opened Milan fashion week made a compelling case for her favourite outfit, with a skirt the star of every one of the 63 looks – no dresses, no trousers. It won the room over, so expect to see the personality skirt on a high street near you soon.

For the past six years, Miuccia Prada has shared design duties with Belgian designer Raf Simons, 20 years her junior. The arrangement was considered unusual when announced, but the house of Prada has always had a way of spinning gold from quirky ideas, and it has worked. “She had the idea to focus on skirts this time,” Simons explained before this show. “And I said, why not make it an all-skirt show?”

blocks.caption: Composite: Shutterstock

blocks.text: She prefers skirts to dresses because “they give you room for contrast,” Mrs Prada said. The way I think and feel is complicated, contradictory. If I wear something feminine, I want to wear something masculine too. A dress is all one idea, and we are never just one idea.”

The skirts were mostly A-line and to the knee. A grey wool skirt, severe from the front, flashed a polka-dot violet slip from beneath splits at each side. A lemon skirt was slashed with a ribbon of embroidered black tulle. There were pleated leather skirts, and daisy-printed silk under a layer of sheer gauze. Bare legs and minimal, elegant high heels throughout. Sometimes, the skirts were worn with lace bras, sometimes with a sweater, elsewhere with a shirt. “Whether you want to go to work, or be sexy, or be relaxed with your kids, you can wear the skirt with whatever you choose,” Simons said.

Fashion usually does its talking from the waist up: a slogan T-shirt, a collar and tie, a plunging neckline. Prada’s personality skirt flips the script. “I like my clothes to have ideas,” Mrs Prada explained backstage, “but I don’t want those ideas near my face, because then they get in the way when I am trying to speak. I think of a skirt the way some people think of a T-shirt – a place to express what I think.”

blocks.caption: Composite: Shutterstock

blocks.text: The Prada empire now extends to ownership of one-time rival, Versace. Donatella Versace, who stepped down from her family brand last year, announced on the eve of Milan fashion week that she was launching a new brand. At 71, Versace remains one of the most popular personalities in fashion, with a 12.2 million Instagram following that dwarfs that of most younger designers. She is partnering with California-based Revolve Inc, whose businesses include a joint venture with rapper Cardi B, for an as-yet-unnamed brand that will launch beauty products next year, with fashion further down the line.

There will be no Versace show this Milan fashion week, with new designer Pieter Mulier, newly arrived from Alaïa, preparing for a debut next season instead. Armani, which last week announced the appointment of young designer Dario Vitale to the Emporio Armani brand, positioning him as an eventual successor to the late Giorgio, is also in transition.
after newsletter promotion

This state of flux is unusual for Milan. Power in Italian fashion has long been concentrated in family-run fashion dynasties, creating a quasi-hereditary-peerage system in which the establishment are deeply invested in the status quo. Paris fashion is where audacious moguls place big bets, London is where young talents experiment, but Milan has favoured stability. But with upheaval at several headline houses – the powerful Fendi matriarchy have also stepped back and appointed Maria Grazia Chiuri to lead their brand – that trend is changing.

articles.title: Congressman Gato of Batanes dies, 66
articles.summary: The incumbent congressman from the lone district of Batanes died on Monday due to cardiac arrest. He was 66.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — The incumbent congressman from the lone district of Batanes died on Monday due to cardiac arrest. He was 66.
Rep. Ciriaco Gato Jr., a doctor who also headed the House committee on health, died while en route to Manila for treatment.
Gato, of the Nationalist People’s Coalition, was Batanes representative since 2019. The NPC, now headed by industrialist Ramon Ang of San Miguel Corp., issued a statement.

“The NPC deeply mourns the passing of Rep. Gato, a valued member of the party, a dedicated public servant, and a physician who devoted his life to caring for others. The NPC extends its deepest sympathies and prayers to his loved ones,” it stated.

“Congressman Gato served the people of Batanes with compassion and unwavering dedication. As a medical doctor and chairperson of the House committee on health, he worked tirelessly to improve the health and well-being of Filipinos,” the party added.

“His life of service will be remembered with gratitude and respect. His loss is deeply felt by the people of Batanes, his colleagues in Congress, the NPC and all whose lives he touched. May Congressman Gato rest in eternal peace,” the NPC said.

Speaker Faustino Dy III expressed his deepest sympathies over the passing of Gato, paying tribute to the physician-lawmaker for a life devoted to public service and the welfare of his fellow Filipinos.
“The entire House of Representatives extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of Congressman Ciriaco Gato,” he said.
Special elections
Meanwhile, the Commission on Elections is eyeing Dec. 19 for the special election in Batanes following Gato’s death, Comelec Chairman George Erwin Garcia said yesterday.
Garcia said the proposal on the schedule for the special election would be submitted to the Comelec next week.
“More or less, the initial date is Dec. 19, if that will be approved,” the Comelec chief said in an interview. — Christine Boton

articles.title: Metro Manila rainwater impounding facilities to cost P4 billion
articles.summary: The five proposed rainwater impounding facilities in Metro Manila can store up to 107,600 cubic meters of rainwater and would require more than P4 billion in funding, according to Executive Secretary…

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:00am
The Office of the Executive Secretayr (OES) on Sept. 22, 2026
Photo from OES

MANILA, Philippines — The five proposed rainwater impounding facilities in Metro Manila can store up to 107,600 cubic meters of rainwater and would require more than P4 billion in funding, according to Executive Secretary Ralph Recto.

The facilities to be administered by the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) form part of ongoing measures to enhance flood mitigation and boost the capital region’s capacity to manage heavy rainfall.

“These impounding facilities will give Metro Manila additional capacity to catch and temporarily store large volumes of rainwater instead of allowing them to immediately overwhelm our drainage systems and flood our communities,” Recto said in a statement.
“When completed, these projects will help protect homes, schools, businesses and public infrastructure, especially during heavy rainfall and high tide,” he added.
The projects will be situated at Camp Aguinaldo, Miriam College, Remedios Circle, Rajah Sulayman Park and the ASEAN Garden at the Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex along Vito Cruz.

“Combined, the five facilities are designed to store up to 107,600 cubic meters of rainwater, providing additional flood water retention capacity in densely populated and flood-prone sections of Metro Manila,” Recto’s office said.
“The five projects have a combined indicative cost of about P4.05 billion, subject to the applicable government review, approval, budgeting and procurement processes,” it added.

The funding for the facilities is proposed under the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management-Disaster Rehabilitation and Reconstruction Assistance Program. MMDA Chairman Romando Artes has submitted documents covering four of the proposed projects to Marcos through Recto’s office and the budget department.

The Camp Aguinaldo facility can cover a 172-hectare catchment area and store up to 50,000 cubic meters of water, while the proposed project at Miriam College will have a 30,000-cubic-meter capacity and serve a 170-hectare catchment area.

The Remedios Circle and Rajah Sulayman Park facilities will have storage capacities of 10,000 cubic meters and 8,000 cubic meters, respectively. Each will serve a 94-hectare catchment area. The flood mitigation project at the ASEAN Garden has a planned capacity of 9,600 cubic meters and can cover a 60-hectare catchment area.
The five projects are among the 39 priority sites for rainwater catchment structures designed to ease the flooding problem in Metro Manila. — Josiah Antonio

articles.title: Philippines developing options on vessel ramming by China
articles.summary: The Philippines is “developing options” to address the ramming of a Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources vessel by a China Coast Guard ship last Friday off Palawan, Defense Secretary…

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is “developing options” to address the ramming of a Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) vessel by a China Coast Guard (CCG) ship last Friday off Palawan, Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro said.

“This definitely needs to be addressed and we’ll be talking with the National Security Adviser and the National Maritime Council,” Teodoro said in an interview on the sidelines of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus Experts’ Working Group on Maritime Security’s Joint Cooperative Activity and Future Leaders’ Program in Olongapo City, Zambales on Monday.
“This is an unarmed vessel, a BFAR vessel. There’s no rhyme, no reason,” he said, referring to the BRP Datu Magat Salamat.

“It’s not merely a violation of maritime rules and regulations, but a criminal act by Chinese Coast Guard. So, we will be addressing that. I’m not going to talk about specifics now, but definitely… our personnel are already developing options for addressing this,” he said.
Asked about some Filipinos defending the CCG’s action against the BFAR vessel, Teodoro said “that is not acceptable, and a betrayal of the Republic of the Philippines.”

In an interview with “Storycon” on One News, Philippine Coast Guard spokesman for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said it was the first recorded case of a Chinese ship deliberately ramming an unarmed civilian Philippine vessel.

“This is the first time that we have documented a China Coast Guard vessel aggressively ramming a government vessel from the Philippines that is unarmed, civilian and conducting a humanitarian mission,” Tarriela said.

“It is only 54 nautical miles from Palawan. That is what is surprising about this particular incident,” he said. “They were really caught by surprise. They were not prepared for this intentional ramming.”
He said it would be illogical for the smaller BFAR vessel to intentionally put itself in the path of a much larger Chinese ship.
“I do not think that vessel would intentionally ram itself because its ship is small compared with the Chinese vessel. It would sink,” he said.
Tarriela said he is not authorized to disclose details of any proposed government response but stressed he is in favor of strengthening the country’s maritime capabilities.
“What we need are more Coast Guard assets and more BFAR assets,” he said.
‘China wants new world media order’

In its latest “Propaganda Monitor” released on Monday, the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) meanwhile has warned of China’s worldwide campaign to shape the media to advance its political and economic interests.
The RSF said Chinese leader Xi Jinping has pursued since 2013 a “new world media order” designed to promote Beijing’s narrative while suppressing reporting that challenges the Chinese government.
The group says the campaign uses everything from media partnerships and foreign-language broadcasting to pursue its goals.

The RSF cited Beijing’s content-sharing deals with foreign broadcasters, funding and equipment for local newsrooms, recruitment of diaspora media, government-backed journalist training and fully funded trips to China.
It also pointed to Chinese embassies’ alleged efforts to discredit or intimidate journalists investigating Beijing’s influence – including cases in the Philippines.

The report also highlights the expanding role of Chinese state media like CGTN and Xinhua which operate in 160 countries. Chinese state-linked institutions, meanwhile, increasingly court YouTubers, TikTok creators and other influencers to reach younger audiences.

Beijing has also targeted independent and diaspora journalists overseas, including those in Uyghur as well as Hong Kong journalists based in the United States and the United Kingdom. With its arrest and detention of 120 news professionals, China can be considered the world’s leading jailer of journalists, according to RSF.

It also warned that China’s information strategy increasingly intersects with other authoritarian governments. Chinese state media organizations such as CGTN, for instance, have amplified material from Russian state outlets including RT and Sputnik, including coverage surrounding Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Such cooperation could help authoritarian governments expand their influence over the global information environment, according to RSF. — Mark Ernest Villeza, Artemio Dumlao

articles.summary: The proposed P785.2-million 2027 budget of the Office of Vice President – which is 11.7 percent lower than this year’s P889.2 million allotment – breezed through House plenary…

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:00am

Office of the Vice President Undersecretary Zuleika Lopez (3rd from left), also the chief of staff of Vice President Sara Z. Duterte, attends the budget hearing of the House of Representatives Committee on Appropriations on Sept. 2, 2026.
PNA photo by Joan Bondoc

MANILA, Philippines — The proposed P785.2-million 2027 budget of the Office of Vice President – which is 11.7 percent lower than this year’s P889.2 million allotment – breezed through House plenary deliberations without any interpellations yesterday.

OVP assistant chief of staff Lemuel Ortonio represented the agency before lawmakers, after his boss, chief of staff Zuleika Lopez submitted a medical certificate asking to be excused from the deliberations.

“We don’t want anything unwelcome to crop up... They were already asking questions during the briefing. It’s just the same. There’s nothing to worry about,” House appropriations committee vice chair and Palawan Rep. Jose Alvarez said during yesterday’s budget hearing.
Alvarez expressed belief that the matter has nothing to do with the ongoing impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte.
“We will not look into whether or not she is impeached. The budget is the budget,” he noted. — Evelyn Macairan

articles.title: P27.4 billion extra MAIFIP fund to benefit 5 million families
articles.summary: An estimated five million families will benefit from the additional P27.41-billion funding allocated for the Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients or MAIFIP program,…

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:00am
Undated photo of medical equipment in a hospital.
The Philippine STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — An estimated five million families will benefit from the additional P27.41-billion funding allocated for the Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients or MAIFIP program, according to the Department of Health (DOH).
The current beneficiaries of the program stand at five million families, Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said yesterday.

“Based on our estimate, with the additional funds given, that would also be the number of families and patients we’ll be able to assist,” Mercado said during an interview with the Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon program.

The DOH chief said that bulk or 70 percent of this P27.41 billion, which is equivalent to P19.145 billion, will be used by centers for health development (CHDs), particularly by local government units (LGUs) and private hospitals under these CHDs.

“This amount can be used in emergency as well as catastrophic cases wherein medical expenses are already too high and PhilHealth coverage is not enough. Though we still recommend for the patient to use PhilHealth first and in our order of billing, you can get a discount depending if one falls under the senior citizen or person with disability category,” explained Mercado.

Meanwhile, the remaining amount of the MAIFIP budget was divided among DOH hospitals in Manila (P4.35 billion), GOCC specialty hospitals including the Lung Center, National Kidney and Transplant Institute, Philippine Children’s Medical Center and Philippine Heart Center (P2.9 billion), UP-Philippine General Hospital (P950 million), and drug abuse treatment and rehabilitation center (P52 million).

Over 70 medical and health care groups have called for the abolition of MAIFIP, calling it a medical pork barrel. The groups said the amount for the politicized health ayuda should instead be given to the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. for expanded PhilHealth services.

articles.title: Government OKs P2.48 billion project to upgrade national ID system
articles.summary: The government has approved a P2.48-billion public-private partnership project to further develop and enhance the national identification system, the Philippine Statistics Authority said yesterday.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:00am

A man gets his eyes scanned as part of the registration for his national ID at a Philippine Statistics Authority booth at the Quezon Memorial Circle in Quezon City, in this file photo from September 2024.
Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The government has approved a P2.48-billion public-private partnership project to further develop and enhance the national identification system, the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) said yesterday.

The Philippine Digital National Identity (PDNI) project secured clearance from the Investment Coordination Committee-Cabinet Committee, chaired by the Department of Finance and co-chaired by the Department of Economy, Planning and Development.
With the approval, the project will move to the procurement stage, where a competitive challenge will be conducted to allow other firms to submit offers for the project.

The competitive challenge is required because the PDNI is an unsolicited proposal from Unisys Public Sector Services Corp., the project’s original proponent. The government will invite competing offers until the fourth quarter of this year, with Unisys retaining the right to match the best offer.
The project will be implemented through a build-transfer-operate arrangement and will cover the upgrade, operation and maintenance of the national ID system.

It will include registration, card production, authentication services, technical onboarding and integration of private-sector relying parties, as well as the operation of the national ID system’s key information and communications technology infrastructure.
The project will have a 20-year concession following a six-month transition period.
Established in 2018 under the Philippine Identification System Act, the national ID aims to provide a single national identification system for all citizens and residents of the country.
Its implementation, however, has faced challenges, including delays in the rollout of physical ID cards.
In 2024, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas terminated its contract with All Card Inc. for failing to fulfill its commitments to supply national ID cards.

The PSA earlier said the government would deliver the physical cards as required under the law, while the printed electronic Philippine ID and digital national ID remain valid forms of identification.

articles.title: No dividends: Defense argument strengthens prosecution's case --Adiong
articles.summary: “Why did the Vice President declare that all these companies who have not consistently [been] declaring dividends can actually justify the increase of her net worth?" said Rep. Adiong.

blocks.text: VP SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT
Published September 22, 2026 11:17pm

The impeachment defense team’s argument that the law does not mandate the declaration of dividends bolsters the prosecution’s assertion that Vice President Sara Duterte’s increase in net worth cannot be accounted for by the business interests she declared in her SALN, the prosecution panel said.

“That [Corporation Code invoked by the defense] is irrelevant and immaterial. He went through a lot of technical details, processes under the revised corporate law but it does not answer one very basic and simple question: Where did the Vice President get all the money reflected in her SALN?” House prosecution panel spokesperson Zia Adiong of Lanao del Sur said in a press conference.

“And why did the Vice President declare that all these companies who have not consistently [been] declaring dividends can actually justify the increase of her net worth?...It even further strengthened the case of the prosecution na hindi iyon ang source of income niya [that these businesses are not the source of her income],” Adiong added.

Impeachment trial defense counsel Justin Gular on Tuesday defended the absence of declared dividends of 10 businesses linked to Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio, saying the law does not require the declaration of dividends.

Gular invoked Section 42 of the Corporation Code, which states that “the board of directors of a stock corporation may declare dividends out of the unrestricted retained earnings which shall be payable in cash, property, or in stock to all stockholders on the basis of outstanding stock held by them.”

Gular then asked prosecution witness SEC Company Registration and Monitoring Department Director Gerardo del Rosario: “So as a lawyer and as an officer of the SEC, you confirm that just because a corporation has unrestricted retained earnings, it’s not automatically required by law para mag-declare ng dibidendo [to declare dividends]. Tama po ba? [Would that be correct?]”
Del Rosario replied, "Tama po." (That’s correct.)

Later in the day, prosecution witness and Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) Division Chief Rendell Sopeña told the Senate impeachment court that GenCorp. Industries Inc, listed by the Vice President as one of her business interest in her 2024 and 2025 Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth, won P35 million worth of government contracts when Duterte was Vice President.
Sopeña said that the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) Region 11 awarded 33 contracts to GenCorp.
Davao City government, on the other hand, also awarded 15 contracts to GenCorp.
The Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) Region 11, for its part, awarded one contract of GenCorp. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from a drug overdose
articles.summary: The death of the child star - who had fentanyl, Xanax, a muscle relaxant and antipsychotic medication in her system - was ruled an accident.

blocks.text: Child star Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed by the Greenville County Coroner's Office in South Carolina.
The coroner's office said Panettiere's death was an accident and that no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to her death.
Panettiere died last month at the age of 36 after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina residence.
The star of US TV shows Heroes and Nashville had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse.
The coroner's office also found methocarbamol - a prescription muscle relaxant - and quetiapine - an antipsychotic medication that is used to treat certain mental health conditions.

items: Drugs at their fingertips, intense pressure: Why child stars fall into addiction

blocks.text: Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone.
The coroner's office said emergency responders had "initiated advanced cardiac life support measures; however, resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful".
The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) was reportedly joining the local police department's investigation into the child star's death.

Panettiere's ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report from the day she died.
Just months before her death, Panettiere published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction and postpartum depression.

articles.title: As Trump and Zelenskyy talk about potential energy truce, Russia and Ukraine unleash new wave of strikes
articles.summary: Ukraine and Russia traded fresh strikes on their respective energy infrastructure overnight, underscoring the gap between the high-level talk of an energy ceasefire in the ongoing war and the reality…

image.caption: A worker with DTek, Ukraine's biggest private energy firm, fixes some infrastructure damaged by Russian strikes in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv. The work is part of preparation for the winter, as Moscow is expected to keep pounding the country's energy grid. (Angela Johnston/CBC)

blocks.text: Ukraine and Russia traded fresh strikes on their respective energy infrastructure overnight, underscoring the gap between the high-level talk of an energy ceasefire in the ongoing war and the reality on the ground.

Ukraine struck two Russian oil refineries, while Russia launched a barrage of missiles at southern Ukraine, hitting several targets, including an oil and gas facility that officials say is now so badly damaged it cannot be restored.
The strikes come as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy prepares to meet U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The two leaders spoke by phone on Sunday, and Trump reportedly raised concerns several times about soaring diesel prices. Zelenskyy said afterward that there are “ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps.”
But Zelenskyy has also said any agreement must protect Ukraine’s food exports and critical infrastructure, not just energy facilities.

items: Putin's ruling party romps to win in wartime Russian election
Norway PM 'prepared, but not afraid' of Russian incursion

blocks.text: The Kremlin has previously said it is open to a moratorium on attacks against energy infrastructure, but has insisted that Western sanctions must also be lifted.
Last week, Trump said both sides had agreed to an energy ceasefire. But the agreement appeared to exist largely on his social media feed, because strikes continued.
For many Ukrainians, this has left little reason for optimism.

“I don't really believe in it, I don't, because there are rockets flying,” said Mykola Nechyporenko, a 55-year-old energy worker who spoke to CBC News as he and a crew repaired a damaged electrical cable in Kyiv on Tuesday, ahead of the winter.
“This whole process is uncontrollable.”
Strikes deepen pressure on Russia's fuel supply
Overnight, Ukraine hit a refinery in Russia’s Samara region, about 500 kilometres southeast of Moscow, as well as a refinery in Ufa, more than 1,100 km from the capital.
Those strikes followed what Moscow's mayor called Ukraine's largest drone attack yet on the capital. On the weekend, Kyiv launched more than 400 drones at a refinery in the city.
The moment a Russian drone bypassed Ukrainian air defences

The attacks are part of a broader Ukrainian campaign against Russia’s energy infrastructure. In recent months, repeated strikes have contributed to fuel shortages, prompting Moscow to ban diesel exports and begin importing fuel from other countries, including India.

In a recent report, the International Energy Agency (IEA) says Russia’s gasoline output is down 20 per cent compared with 2025 levels, while diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30 per cent.
The IEA says Russia has 32 major refineries, some of which have been attacked as many as 15 times since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In the first eight months of 2026, a Russian refinery was hit, on average, once every three days, according to the agency.
The disruption is being felt by Russian drivers. Videos posted on social media have shown shortages at gas stations, with frustration at times boiling over into fistfights at the pumps.
The pressure on fuel supplies has also contributed to higher diesel prices internationally, according to the IEA.
Russia targets Ukraine's energy system
While Ukraine strikes deep inside Russia, Moscow has kept up its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Overnight, Russia launched several ballistic missiles at southern Ukraine, including at an energy facility in the Poltava region.
Ukraine struggles to defend against Russian jet-powered drones

The facility is owned by Naftogaz, Ukraine’s largest oil and gas company. The company said at least five missiles struck the site. It had already been shut down, but Naftogaz said the latest damage was so severe that it would no longer be possible to restore and operate the facility.
The state-owned company also operates a network of gas stations, called Ukrnafta. Some are now being fortified with barriers in an effort to reduce damage if they come under attack.
Russia has already targeted several gas stations with drones, including one in the city of Boryspil on Aug. 20.

“There was an alert, and we went with the others behind the petrol station and then there was an explosion in the air and shrapnel came down,” said Valentyn Krasnopir, 63, whose leg was severely injured in the strike. He spoke to CBC News on Saturday from a hospital bed in Kyiv.
Krasnopir said he has lost hope in negotiations.
Iryna Panina, 36, feels the same sense of exhaustion. She was startled awake overnight by what she described as the sound of an aircraft falling, followed by a large explosion.

The windows in her apartment were blown out and furniture was thrown across the floor when a neighbouring five-storey building was hit in the attack. The first floor of that building caught on fire. Two people were injured, and all of the residents were evacuated.

On Tuesday afternoon, as residents gathered alongside emergency crews to try and start the cleanup, air defences rang out in the Ukrainian capital as crews attempted to shoot down a swarm of Russian drones.
“This war has continued too long for us. I don't know what to say, because we are all tired of this and we want some peace,” Panina said in an interview with CBC News.
“I think most of us don't believe in these [Trump/Zelenskyy] meetings. Just talking … that's all. I don't think that something will change.”
New challenge for Ukraine's air defences
The latest attacks come as Ukraine faces another challenge on the battlefield: Russia’s use of jet-powered drones.

Kyiv has adopted a strategy of sending multiple waves of drones toward a target at once in an effort to overwhelm Russian air defences. But Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones, which travel too quickly for some of the country’s existing systems.
Ukraine launches 'largest ever' attack on Moscow
The attacks have raised concerns about another difficult winter if Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy grid.
“It's like a neverending story,” said Panina.
“I think we will make some damage for [the Russians], they will for us, and how long it takes? I don't know."

articles.title: Veteran BBC Africa correspondent Mark Doyle dies
articles.summary: Doyle was best known for reporting on African conflicts in the 1990s and 2000s, notably in Rwanda and Sierra Leone.

blocks.text: British journalist Mark Doyle, best known for his reporting on conflicts in Africa in the 1990s and 2000s, has died after a short illness.
After living in Africa, he joined the BBC in 1986. Doyle became East Africa correspondent in 1993 and made his mark covering the Rwandan genocide a year later.
As West Africa correspondent from 1997 to 2002, he reported on Sierra Leone's brutal civil war and aftermath of Liberia's conflict.
Following Doyle's death, BBC foreign editor Paul Danahar said he was a "legendary figure", as well as a" brilliant, brave, empathetic reporter".
The BBC's Andrew Harding, who worked with Doyle, paid tribute to his former colleague in a 2015 article, published to mark his departure from the national broadcaster.

In the piece Fergal Keane, another prominent BBC correspondent in Africa, recalled their stint in Rwanda in 1994. "He stayed longer than any of us," Keane said of Doyle. "Those who were in that awful place at that awful time will know what Mark Doyle gave for the cause of truth and for the BBC."
In the same article Sir David Richards, who headed British forces struggling to stop Sierra Leone's civil war in 2000, also praised Doyle.

Sir David said his reporting helped convince the UK government of the need for a robust intervention. "Hence the saving of thousands of Sierra Leonean lives that would otherwise have been at huge risk," he said.
In 2004 Doyle won first prize in the UN Correspondents Association/UN Foundation Awards for his coverage of post-war Liberia.
He became BBC World Affairs correspondent before retiring from the BBC in 2015.

articles.title: Military aircraft crashes near US air base in Spangdahlem, Germany
articles.summary: The Spangdahlem Air Base is located in the German state of Rhineland-Palatinate. Local authorities said that first responders were helping at the scene but that they could only comment in a limited…

image.caption: Spangdahlem Air base is located in western Germany, near the Luxembourg border.Image: Harald Tittel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A military aircraft has crashed near the US air base in Spangdahlem, Germany, on Tuesday.
The plane crash occurred at approximately 2.30 pm local time (12:30 UTC). The cause of the incident is currently under investigation.
The US military confirmed that the plane was an F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing and that its pilot was able to safely eject from the aircraft.
Local authorities in the remote Eifel region also reported that one person had been injured.

"Following a plane crash in the vicinity of US Air Base Spangdahlem, fire and emergency response teams from the Eifel District of Bitburg-Prüm were dispatched to the scene," the district said on its website.
"No comments can be made on the further details of the event from the side of the Eifel district at this time."
A NATO operations center

Spangdahlem Air Base is a NATO operations center that was built in the early 1950s. The US Air Force's 52nd Fighter Wing is garrisoned there. The base is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron comprising around 20 aircraft.
It is located north of the city of Trier in Rhineland-Palatinate, not far west of the border to Luxembourg.

blocks.caption: At least one person was injured, authorities saidImage: Harald Tittel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The facility at Spangdahlem is considered one of the most important airfields for the US military in Germany, alongside Ramstein base, outside the city of Kaiserslautern.
Some 5,000 US military and civilian personnel-plus dependents are stationed at Spangdahlem, with around 700 to 800 Germans also employed at the facility.

articles.title: US-China AI race: Does Trump want to regulate AI by forming a new task force and a special envoy for artificial intelligence in the US?
articles.summary: Do Trump's task force and a special envoy for artificial intelligence in the US indicate a move toward regulating this disputed technology, particularly vis-a-vis China?

image.caption: US President Donald Trump has announced a change of course in his AI policyImage: Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Developers warning against their own technologies and a government unwilling to take action — that was the situation in the first half of September amid concerns in the US that AI models were becoming too powerful.
Several developers and decision-makers from major AI companies had also called for slowing down the development of the technology.

In response, US President Donald Trump posted one of his typical all-caps tweets on his social media platform Truth Social: "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX." Trump also asked "Concerning AI, when, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?"

Against this backdrop, it comes as something of a surprise that Trump announced over the weekend — following yet another tirade about various alleged Democratic scams — that he would establish an "AI Force" and appoint a special envoy to address the issue.
What exactly did Trump say?

In his post, Trump promised that he would by no means slow down the industry's growth. "However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System," he wrote. "To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar' — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added.
Trump left open exactly what the individual's duties and powers would be and what resources would be allocated to the position.

Trump's announcement could be an attempt to undermine an initiative by California's Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom. The previous day, Newsom had announced plans to establish a commission to regulate Silicon Valley-based tech companies.

Among other things, Newsom wants to require these companies to build an emergency shut-off switch into their programs, which would allow humans to stop AI agents that have spun out of control. Several states, including some led by Republicans, are pushing for regulation.
US fear of China's dominance

The current "AI race" between the US and China is often compared to the space race between the US and the former Soviet Union in the 1960s. Several US companies are currently considered industry leaders. To ensure this remains the case, Trump intends to continue giving them free rein.
However, this is not just about economic interests. There is concern that Chinese dominance in artificial intelligence could also lead to Beijing's rise as the sole superpower.

In a widely discussed essay, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, not only warned of the consequences of continued unchecked AI development; he also outlined the potential consequences of the AI competition between the US and China.

"If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance. Therefore any agreement must either have ironclad verifiability, or must be limited enough that defection would not be militarily existential," Amodei wrote.

blocks.caption: Tech leaders call for transparency and an emergency switch off for robots and AI technologiesImage: Tingshu Wang/REUTERS

blocks.text: Does China regulate AI?

In China, technological developments have traditionally been much more closely tied to governmental objectives. As early as 2017, the State Council of China issued a development plan for a new generation of artificial intelligence.

Another strategy paper sets out milestones through which China aims to achieve global dominance in the field of AI by 2030. The regulations are primarily enforced by the Chinese Cyberspace Administration (CAC), which also issues licenses.

Regulation in China ensures that AI models do not run counter to official political doctrine. For example, the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek consistently provides answers loyal to the regime when asked politically sensitive questions — such as those regarding Taiwan, the Tiananmen Square massacre, or the oppression of the Uyghurs — as DW previously documented.

The underlying logic of Chinese regulation is thus based on the question: How does an AI system align with state objectives? This represents a clear distinction from the risk-based regulation envisaged, for example, by the European AI Act and now being called for in the US.

blocks.caption: Could the US and China share information on AI technology as discussed between US Minister of Finance Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng? Image: Bai Xueqi/Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Is an AI agreement between the US and China imminent?
On Thursday, Trump will host Chinese President Xi Jinping at a state dinner at the White House. The topic of AI is likely to be very high on the agenda.

The US already proposed establishing a mechanism for exchanging information about serious risks posed by AI. The proposal was discussed at a meeting between Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday in New York.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent said.

Whether they actually decide to act on this will likely be left up to the two presidents. After all, for them, potential transparency obligations regarding AI are by no means the only point of contention in the negotiations.
For years, trade restrictions on high-performance AI chips and rare earth elements have been a recurring issue and the extension of a basic trade agreement is also on the agenda.
Whether mutual trust is strong enough to lead to reciprocal concessions on AI will likely only become clear at the meeting.
This article was originally published in German.
How the US and China could end the AI race

articles.title: Young Berliners vote overwhelmingly for socialist Left Party
articles.summary: Berlin's young voters overwhelmingly supported the victorious socialist Left Party. Are the young more radical? Or is that just a reflection of current German politics?

image.caption: Some 43% of Berlin's 16-24-year-olds voted for the socialist Left PartyImage: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: The emphatic victory for the Left Party in last Sunday's state election in Berlin may not have been quite so emphatic if it hadn't been for a significant new rule: This was the first state election in the German capital's history where the voting age had been lowered from 18 to 16.

The actual change was relatively small: It only added around 55,000 voters to the city's electorate of 2.5 million, but it was massively significant to young people themselves: "Of course we talk a lot about politics at school or among our friends," 17-year-old Cecilia told DW's Franziska Wüst on the street outside her school in Berlin on Monday. "We're all very politically engaged; we go to a lot of demos."
Young socialists

That spirit of protest appears to have been reflected in young Berliners' voting habits. While the official exit poll statistics from infratest-dimap don't isolate under-18s, the age-group breakdowns suggest that the Left Party's voters (some 1 in 4 of Berlin voters) skew young. Some 43% of 16-24-year-olds voted for the socialist party — a huge 25-point leap on the last state election in 2023.

That makes sense to 17-year-old Liska, who voted for the socialists: "The Left Party did appeal to me, especially because of the social issues — getting prices down, making rents more affordable." Rents in Berlin are indeed rising at a massive pace — by some 7% in the last two years alone — and first-time tenants are likely to be the hardest hit. Polls also showed that by far the biggest proportion of Berlin voters — 37% — thought that the Left Party was the most likely to create affordable housing.

Cecilia also agreed that rents, as well as the conservative Berlin government's plans to cut education budgets, were the overwhelming concerns among her friends. "We're all getting to an age where we'd kind of like to move out, which in Berlin is almost impossible," she said. "Otherwise, of course it's issues like school, education, so it doesn't get cut everywhere."
Young radicals?

All those answers make a lot of sense to Kathrin Fehse of the German Children's and Youth Foundation (DKJS), which represents the interests of Germany's young people. "It's all the issues that affect them personally," she told DW. "And for that they need to be taken seriously and asked. And the Left Party was one of the parties that mobilized a lot of non-voters, not just young voters — they're people that politicians were not addressing before."

Throughout the campaign, the Left Party had been portrayed as dangerous radicals by the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the party of the incumbent mayor, Kai Wegner — however true that is, it did not appear to scare off young voters.

Some argue that young people are more likely to vote for the radical ends of the spectrum. Cecilia can see that point: "I think that it's generally true that young people are always a lot more extreme than the older generations, and I do see that too, that it's always very extreme opinions," she said.

But there's also evidence that this is something of a stereotype: Infratest-dimap statistics show the biggest age group for the Left Party were the 25-34-year-olds (some 49% of the vote), while the biggest age group for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the Berlin election were 60-69-year-olds (23%). By comparison, only 12% of 16-24-year-old Berlin voters went for the AfD.
What do young people want?

Gefjon Off, a political scientist who has researched the voting habits of younger generations, said that while it might be generally the case that younger people have more "radical" opinions than older people, the statistical evidence shows that middle-aged men vote for the AfD more than young men. People's age, in other words, "doesn't mean that they are more likely to vote for anti-democratic parties," she said.
German state elections reveal increasingly polarized country

What characterizes young voters is not so much radical views, argued Off, but their looser affiliation to any particular party: "In the federal election in 2021, for example, climate protection was a huge issue, and a lot of young people voted for the Greens as the climate was their issue," she told DW. "In this election, affordable housing was a huge issue for the Left Party. That means young people vote more according to issues, and are easier to move from one party to another."

Off also thinks that young people are less scared off by the stigmatization around the Left Party that still hangs round older generations who associate it with the communist dictatorship of East Germany.

Fehse said that in the DKJS' own study on young people's opinion, named VoiceUp, was that, "Young people want solidarity, participation, positive prospects for their future, and at the same time they experience these things much too seldom," she said. "And at the end of the day, those experiences create the social context in which their political decisions are made."
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: Marcoleta: INC's silence on my detention is respect for due process, test of faith
articles.summary: Detained Senator Rodante Marcoleta addressed on Tuesday the perceived “silence” of the religious sect Iglesia Ni Cristo (INC) regarding his imprisonment, saying it reflects respect for due process…

blocks.text: Published September 22, 2026 9:59pm

Detained Senator Rodante Marcoleta addressed on Tuesday the perceived “silence” of the religious sect Iglesia Ni Cristo (INC) regarding his imprisonment, saying it reflects respect for due process and tests their faith.

“This is to dispel the notion circulating on various social media platforms today that the perceived ‘silence’ of the Iglesia Ni Cristo concerning my imprisonment is in a way equated to the Church’s resolve in approaching the said issue,” Marcoleta wrote in a Facebook post.
Marcoleta is an INC member. During his senatorial campaign, the church endorsed his bid and ultimately stood by him when plunder charges were brought against him in July.
Marcoleta said the INC has no obligation to publicly react or comment on his detention, adding that his current situation reflects a test of faith that church members fully understand.

“The INC adheres to what has been foretold: that its members—prominent or otherwise—will not be immune from persecution and privation as these ordeals were palpably chronicled by varied biblical accounts evidencing how their faith was tested to the hilt,” the senator said.

“To be sure, it is the fundamental doctrine of the Church that all that is bound to happen is willed by God according to His plan which, in the end, will ultimately redound to the flock’s good and betterment,” he added.
According to Marcoleta, the INC is no stranger to public vilification and views these trials as a rite of passage that tests each member’s faith and moral integrity.
Marcoleta emphasized that the silence of the INC should not be mistaken for weakness or a lack of resolve.

“The INC’s “silence” on my jailing should never be misconstrued as indifference, weakness, or diminished resolve. It reflects neither acquiescence nor abandonment but fidelity to its deep-seated beliefs and respect for the judicial processes,” he added.
Marcoleta is currently detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas for his pending non-bailable plunder case.

The Office of the Ombudsman filed the plunder charges after finding that Marcoleta received P75 million in campaign contributions for the 2025 senatorial elections, which he failed to declare in his Statement of Contributions and Expenditures. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate juror and check his phone
articles.summary: The attorney wants the court to look at the juror's mobile phone use and answers on questionnaires.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Lindsay Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington made several attempts to convince the judge not to declare a mistrial
The defence lawyer for a Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three children has asked a judge to investigate a juror in the case.
The proceedings against Lindsay Clancy ended in a mistrial and acrimony this month after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
Her attorney, Kevin Reddington, wants the court to probe mobile phone use by "Juror Doe" during deliberations as well as a questionnaire he filled out.

A lawyer for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who wanted to find Clancy guilty, said the latest defence motion was a "Looney Tunes" attack on his client for doing his civic duty. Desronvil has said there was "enough proof that she [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing".
Watch: Patrick Clancy says he forgives his ex-wife, Lindsay
Warning: This article contains distressing details
The juror forewoman has claimed in a media interview that Desronvil had expressed reasonable doubt about Clancy's guilt, which would require him to find her not guilty. He denies this.
Clancy has not denied killing her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home.
Her attorneys argued she was not guilty by reason of insanity, that she was struggling with postpartum psychosis at the time.
Prosecutors said Clancy made a calculated decision to send her husband out of the house on an errand so she could strangle her children.
In his motion filed on Friday, Reddington asked the court to look at calls and texts that "Juror Doe" made between 08:00 and 16:30 local time during all the days the jury deliberated.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cora, five, Callan, eight months, and Dawson, three

blocks.text: Image source, The Heard Foundation
Cora, five, Callan, eight months, and Dawson, three
He also asked the court to examine the truthfulness of the answers the juror gave during the jury selection process, as well as his responses to prospective juror questionnaires.
In a separate motion, Reddington also asked for the case against Clancy to be dismissed. Prosecutors have yet to say whether they will retry her.
Facing a backlash for refusing to acquit Clancy, Desronvil has hired an attorney to represent him.
The lawyer, Edward Paltzik, said in a statement on X that the "disgusting" defence motion was an attack on the US constitutional right to a fair trial.
"If the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye," he wrote.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Desronvil (seen here in a photo provided by his lawyer) has said he had no doubt about Clancy's guilt

blocks.text: Image source, @EdPaltzik
Desronvil (seen here in a photo provided by his lawyer) has said he had no doubt about Clancy's guilt
Several jurors have said after the trial ended that they were ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
Desronvil said last week that he had no doubt about her guilt.

"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
The jury forewoman, a retired fifth-grade teacher, said in an interview with NBC that Desronvil had admitted he had reasonable doubt, but refused to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

articles.title: Up to 169 killed in Yemen as Houthis battle for Red Sea coastal heights
articles.summary: Thousands flee fighting as Iran-aligned group seeks to consolidate territorial gains against Saudi-backed government forces

blocks.text: As many as 169 people have been reportedly killed in Yemen in the last three days as Iran-aligned Houthis battle Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic heights on the Red Sea coast, while thousands flee the violence.

Houthi military officials said at least 118 people had been killed in clashes as well as Saudi air and artillery strikes on Taiz, al-Jawf, Marib and Saada provinces since Sunday, Agence France-Presse reported. Yemeni government sources have said at least 36 people have been killed on their side of the conflict.

The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking the port city of Mocha on Tuesday, killing six civilians, including two children. The group also said a Saudi strike on a prison in al-Jawf province, north-western Yemen, killed nine detainees.

The Saudi government, which backs Yemen’s UN-recognised government against Houthi forces, on Tuesday issued an alert in the south of the country before potential strikes, after the Houthis launched strikes at the Saudi capital, Riyadh, at the weekend for the first time in years.

blocks.caption: A screengrab from AFPTV footage of Saudi-backed government fighters engaging Houthi forces in al-Jawf province, in the north-west of Yemen. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The renewed fighting came after a dramatic offensive launched by the Houthis three weeks earlier in which the group seized control of much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from government-aligned forces. They were the most significant territorial gains in the last four years of the civil war in the country.

The offensive has upended global energy markets, which are already reeling from the Iranian closure of the strait of Hormuz, and further expanded the regional scope of the US-Iran war, now in its seventh month.

Last week the Houthis took control of Mocha and other strategic cities, which gave them control over the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping lane home to 10% of all global maritime traffic that has gained renewed importance after the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
The clashes have compounded an already dire humanitarian crisis, where about 22 million people need humanitarian assistance and 5.2 million people are already internally displaced.

blocks.caption: Displaced Yemeni people receive medical care at a camp in Ras Imran, a coastal area on the western outskirts of Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: Yemen’s civil war started in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the country’s capital and toppled the government. A Saudi-led coalition then intervened in an aerial campaign on behalf of the internationally recognised Yemeni government and allied militias.
A UN-brokered ceasefire was established in 2022, which had largely held until the Houthis launched the current offensive.

In recent days, clashes have focused on the strategic Kahboub mountains near the Red Sea coast as the Houthis seek to consolidate recent territorial gains. Government forces have been trying to hold the line against the Houthi advance on multiple fronts to prevent them from seizing the mountain range.

Control of the mountains would give the Houthis a strategic vantage point over Red Sea coastal areas and would further cut off Aden, the seat of Yemeni government forces, from the western coast. Seizing the mountains would also complicate future government counterattacks.

The Houthis have advanced on multiple fronts, particularly the outskirts of Taiz province and the coastal area of Ras al-Ara, with the greater goal of controlling the Kahboub mountains. Media affiliated with the Houthis have reported gains in the area, while government media said its fighters had successfully repelled Houthi incursions.

blocks.caption: Houthi-aligned detainees arrive in Sana’a after being freed from prisons run by Saudi-backed forces in Mocha after Houthis made gains in the region. Photograph: Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images

blocks.text: Since the Houthi campaign was launched, the group has routed government-aligned forces from western Yemen. The prospect of an Iranian-aligned force controlling Bab al-Mandeb has worried Saudi Arabia as it would place two shipping lanes vital to its energy exports in the hands of Iran and its allies.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes on Yemen in recent days to try to stop the Houthis, with little success.

Donald Trump reportedly considered striking the Houthis over the weekend but called them off at the last minute, while the UK said it would assist aerial refuelling of Saudi aircraft engaged in defensive missions, leaving open the prospect of further international intervention.

Members of the G7 have called on Iran to stop arming the Houthis. In a joint statement released ahead of the UN general assembly, member states urged the Houthis to stop their strikes on Saudi Arabia, which have damaged key oil infrastructure and wounded dozens.
“We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith,” the statement read.

The clashes have killed about 700 people and displaced more than 100,000 people, pushing some Yemenis to flee the fighting via sea. Civilians have fled westwards across the Red Sea to Djibouti, while aid groups warn conditions for those remaining in Yemen are deteriorating.

blocks.caption: People fleeing the fighting queue to receive supplies after crossing the Red Sea and arriving in Djibouti. Photograph: Abdourahim Arteh/Reuters

blocks.text: Babar Baloch, a UN refugee agency spokesperson, said on Tuesday that displacement inside Yemen could rise to 230,000 people and more than 10,000 could flee to Djibouti if fighting continued.

Saudi Arabia has tried to marshal international support to roll back the Houthi offensive, with the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking Trump to strike the Houthis – a request Trump has thus far refused.

Trump held a call with the head of Yemen’s governing body, Rashad al-Alimi, on Monday, with al-Alimi asking the US for military assistance. Trump expressed solidarity but did not promise military support, a source told Agence France-Presse.

articles.title: British banks told not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins
articles.summary:
MPs send out letter as Israeli government seeks bids for construction of large E1 settlement in West Bank

British banks and financial institutions are receiving written warnings from MPs…

blocks.text: British banks and financial institutions are receiving written warnings from MPs that they should not invest in Israel’s E1 settlement project even though new UK laws banning trade with illegal settlements are unlikely to be in place for months.
A letter was sent to banks on Tuesday by the all-party Britain-Palestine group of MPs saying the onus was now on banks to review their obligations not to cooperate with new settlements.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced two weeks ago plans for a complete ban on trade with illegal settlements and new sanctions on those co-operating with building the settlements. But complex secondary legislation needed for the powers to come into force may take six to nine months to pass through parliament.

The issue is urgent since the Israeli government is seeking bids for two tenders for the construction of as many as 3,400 houses, including more than 1,300 for which the tender closes on 25 October, two days before the elections.

Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said in 2025 that the E1 settlement “practically erases the two-state delusion” by splitting up territory that would be set aside for a Palestinian state. The settlement plan has long been delayed due to its uncontested political impact on the prospect of a two-state solution, still the main peace plan backed by the west and Gulf states.

blocks.caption: Israel’s far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, holding a map showing the proposed E1 settlement. Photograph: Menahem Kahana/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Finance, insurance and guarantees are required before construction starts. One of Miliband’s motives in acting earlier this month, before the Israeli elections, was not just to express his deep concern at the scale of settler violence in the West Bank but to deter UK finance from helping with the tenders or the construction. It has been alleged that he overrode some diplomatic advice in acting before the elections.

The all-party group said: “The immediate question is what commitments institutions were willing to make while the detailed rules are being developed, and how they would respond when restrictions take effect”. The letter, signed by two Labour MPs, Debbie Abrahams and Andy McDonald, states: “Commitments made now may be difficult to unwind when restrictions commence; the allocation of costs will depend on the contracts and applicable law. We ask boards to consider this interim risk before agreeing new or increased commitments.”

The letter adds: “We ask you to place potential E1 and settlement-related exposure on the board’s agenda and on the risk register, and to reach a reasoned decision on whether the associated sanctions, legal and reputational risk sits within the institution’s stated risk appetite.”
It is argued that postcodes provide the locality of a product’s origin, and nothing is being attempted that would stop trade in general with Israel.

Abrahams said: “We are not asking to pre-empt the law. We are asking boards a question they should be able to answer today: what exposure are you prepared to carry while the sanctions regime is written and on what evidence?”
The all-party group said it intended to publish replies to its letter by 10 October.
