articles.title: Turkey: Several pupils injured in shooting outside school
articles.summary: The shooter, a pupil, allegedly took a rifle and shot indiscriminately at his schoolmates in front of their high school. Turkey was shocked by two back-to-back school shootings earlier this year.

image.caption: Footage posted online showed a male carrying a rifle near the schoolImage: DHA

blocks.text: A shooting near a high school in Turkey's Manisa province resulted in at least 11 injured pupils, two of whom were in critical condition on Tuesday, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said.
The shooter, a pupil at the school, was arrested together with both of his parents and his grandfather.
What do we know about the shooting incident?
The suspect is said to have taken the weapon from his grandparents' house, with his grandfather believed to have had a licence for it.
Local authorities said the attack took place at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the Turgutlu district at about 08:00am local time (07:00 CET).
The motive for the shooting is also under investigation. Some reports suggest the student had suffered from bullying.

blocks.caption: Two back-to-back school shootings in April left around 10 killed and dozens more injuredImage: Ensar Ozdemir/REUTERS

blocks.text: "When the ​security of our children is the issue, it is not possible for any ​negligence, any irresponsibility to be overlooked," the minister posted on his X account.

"The ‌circumstances under which the child obtained the gun used in the attack, the conditions of the weapon's storage, the parents' obligations regarding care ‌and supervision, and allegations of bullying prior to the incident ‌are ​being investigated thoroughly and from multiple angles," Gurlek added.
Footage posted online showed a male carrying a rifle near the school, while police told families to stay away from the area.
Gun control tightened after school shootings
School shootings are rare in Turkey, but this year alone saw two back-to-back shootings that shocked the nation.
Two school shootings that took place in April resulted in the tightening of gun controls and the increase of security measures at educational facilities as the academic year started last week.
Several students and their teacher were killed in one of the attacks, with the other resulting in 16 people being injured.
According to Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci, 31,000 school supervisors and police officers on duty were assigned to school seen as being at risk, as per a new measure introduced only on Monday.
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan responded to the latest shooting attack by promising even tighter gun controls.
"When we look at similar attacks around the world, especially in the United States, we see one of the perpetrators' aims is to terrorise society," the Turkish leader said.

articles.title: Jollibee enters the menu as impeach court scrutinizes Sara Duterte businesses
articles.summary: 'Bida ang sarap, bida ang ebidensya,' prosecutor Terry Ridon quips

blocks.text: Graphics by Nico Villarete/Rappler
'Bida ang sarap, bida ang ebidensya,' prosecutor Terry Ridon quips
Even the country’s top fast food chain was not spared in the expansive investigation into Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.
Could Jollibee hold a piece of the smoking gun that the prosecution has been searching for to remove her from office?

Jollibee was implicated in the mess because documents show that its Bolton Street branch in Davao City is owned by Gencorp Industries Inc., described in one of government documents as a franchisee of the casual dining giant.

Duterte said in her sworn Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) that she is a stockholder of Gencorp, although her name is not in Securities and Exchange Commission documents (SEC) filings of the company.

Other companies associated with the Vice President or her husband Mans Carpio are Metro City Chow Food Corporation, City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation, Timesquare Bee Foods Corp., and Great Jolly Times Food Corp.
The names of several of these companies appear to echo those of Jollibee and its sister fast-food chain, Chowking.

“This P2.1 billion in sales — these are restaurants, right? Are they Jollibee or Chowking?” Senator Kiko Pangilinan asked. “I would assume there are many Jollibee and Chowking franchises, which is why sales reached billions over a period of time.”
“One of the financial statements that the witness identified yesterday contains the word ‘Jollibee’ in reference to Gencorp,” prosecutor Erwin Matib said. “Yes, there are franchises.”
Jollibee Davao Bolton is a known hangout spot of the Dutertes. It is in the same building as the listed address of Gencorp.

Rappler previously reported that Gencorp has cornered at least P14 million in contracts with Davao City Hall since 2022, coinciding with the time that Sara became VP, and her brother Sebastian assumed the mayorship of their hometown.

The Davao City mayor later not only confirmed the existence of the deals, but even updated the actual total value of the contracts bagged by Gencorp — P33 million over 19 contracts. Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System division chief Rendell Sopeña told the impeachment court that there are 15 Gencorp-Davao City deals worth P34 million in its database.

The arrangement raises questions on conflict of interest, and potential violation of the Constitution. The 1987 charter explicitly prohibits the Vice President from having business interests while in office.
The Jollibee connection did not escape the prosecution and her critics, which used its slogan to take a swipe at the Vice President.
“Bida ang sarap, bida ang ebidensiya (the star is the flavor, the star is the evidence),” prosecutor Terry Ridon said.

blocks.caption: Jollibee enters the menu as impeach court scrutinizes Sara Duterte businesses

blocks.text: “Inday, pa-Jollibee ka naman diyan (Inday, how about treating us to Jollibee),” former presidential adviser Ronald Llamas said in jest on Facebook.
Spectators of the trial might just be craving two things after Tuesday’s proceedings: a one-piece Chickenjoy, and an explanation from the Vice President. – Rappler.com

items: 6m agoUS TV networks suspend White House pool coverage over Trump media ban

blocks.text: US TV networks suspend White House pool coverage over Trump media ban
Ariana Baio
The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds.
The collective decision came after the barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights.

The ban was an extraordinary escalation of Trump’s battle against news outlets. After a coalition of networks including ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – which along with CNN form a press “pool” that share the responsibilities of capturing and distributing footage of the president carried by news outlets worldwide – announced they would cease coverage in solidarity with the barred outlets, the White House promoted its own feed online, branding it “Trump TV”. The channel purported to show “top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place”.
“Get real-time updates and live events streamed DIRECTLY to your phone,” the White House posted on social media. “No noise. Just the news that matters most – straight from the Trump Administration.”

It is extremely rare for a president to travel or make public appearances without the accompaniment of a representative from the White House television pool. Network cameras have provided coverage of the president since 1950.

On Monday, the ban against CNN meant that no broadcaster was covering Trump’s midday ribbon-cutting to unveil a new White House helipad. Although the White House provided a livestream, without professional boom mics and audio setup, the president’s remarks were inaudible over the sounds of a helicopter’s engine running in the background.

The president abruptly announced his ban against outlets this weekend in a Truth Social post, saying he had enough of “purposely negative stories” about him. Journalists had their press badges confiscated by Secret Service on Saturday.
Trump set for UN meetings with war on agenda as speech looms
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump is expected to ⁠start the day with a speech to assembled delegates at the UN General Assembly, before meeting with no fewer than 11 world leaders, bilaterally or in group settings.

While the contents of his speech are unknown, Trump last year caused a ⁠stir with a combative address, telling the audience that their countries were “going to hell” for, among other things, climate policy and mass migration.
The president is then set for a whirlwind schedule of meetings with ⁠leaders from four continents on Tuesday.
It comes against the backdrop of an unstable Middle East and a four-and-a-half-year-old war in Ukraine that shows no signs of abating.

Trump will meet with British prime minister Andy Burnham, Ukrainian ‌president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Venezuela’s interim leader Delcy ‌Rodriguez, Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland prime minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and the representatives of the Gulf states of the United Arab Emirates, ‌Saudi Arabia, Oman, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar.

In the evening, he may meet dozens more leaders, albeit briefly, during a leaders’ reception. Trump met with French president Emmanuel Macron on Monday and additions to his Tuesday schedule are possible.
Here, my colleague Robert Tait provides some analysis on what may be expected from Trump’s address:
In other developments:

items: The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds. Newsrooms including the New York Times and the Washington Post also decided to hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage on Monday until midnight as part of the collective effort. More here.

The barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights. The parties are seeking a temporary restraining order that would immediately lift the ban – and return access for the journalists – while the case plays out. More here.

Trump is bracing for a loss in the lawsuit brought by the three media organizations, as he considers that the judge presiding over the case – his own appointee – previously ordered the White House to restore credentials for journalist Jim Acosta. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote on Truth Social.

Trump said that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms. More here.

The Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon when he was able to call his lawyer, in the middle of a press conference, and plead for better medical care. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine and is in much discomfort. More here.

Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Republican subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet, has said the allegations are untrue – and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her. More here.

blocks.text: Russia and Ukraine traded strikes targeting infrastructure overnight, ahead of a United Nations General Assembly where the war in Ukraine is due to be widely discussed.
Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight into Tuesday killed four people, Ukrainian officials said, while also cutting the electricity supply to thousands.

The strikes took place in the cities Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad in the southeastern region of Dnipropetrovsk, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Telegram. The barrage included anti-ship and ballistic missiles, four cruise missiles and 212 drones.
DW witnesses Ukrainian train evacuation
The region of Dnipropetrovsk is the country's industrial heartland, where major production industries are located, including steel-making and machine building.
In the city of Dnipro, four people were killed and six were injured. According to Hanzha, the strike also damaged a local business and a warehouse.
Ukraine strikes Russian oil refinery; 1 killed
In Russia, Ukrainian drones killed one person and injured four in the Samara region, local authorities said. The region is home to important facilities, including oil refineries.
Moscow's Defense Ministry said it had intercepted 297 drones over various regions in Russia overnight.
Samara is located some 1,000 kilometers southeast of Russian capital Moscow.
Zelenskyy attends UN General Assembly
Russia and Ukraine have both stepped up attacks recently, as the war has dragged on for four and a half years with no end in sight.
Both parties deny targeting civilians, while also blaming each other for civilian casualties.

The latest attacks come as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is planning to meet US counterpart Donald Trump in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Russian President Vladimir Putin is not expected at the UN General Assembly.

articles.title: Male infertility is 'grossly underreported'
articles.summary: It's not all on women anymore — doctors do test men for sperm count and motility. But still too few men get checked, possibly due to a misconception that a healthy sex life means healthy sperm.…

image.caption: It just takes one out 16 million sperm, but many men can't even manage that Image: ktsdesign/Panthermedia/IMAGO

blocks.text: Sperm counts have fallen globally by more than 51% since 1973, and the decline is accelerating. That's according to a 2026 review of studies published in the journal Antioxidants. But men are less likely to get tested than women for infertility.
"Male infertility is understated. It is so huge a problem," said Edidiong Akang, a reproductive biologist at the University of Lagos, Nigeria.

In a study led by Akang and published in the journal Scientific Reports in 2023, he and his colleagues analyzed semen samples from more than 17,000 men and found that the quality of sperm shape and size (known as sperm morphology) had deteriorated by about 50% between 2010 and 2019.
Sperm motility (how well it swims to the female egg) had also dropped significantly — in Nigeria, for example, by 87% in that same period.
And yet, as Akang told DW, the male share of infertility is "grossly underreported" and, as a result, misunderstood.
What affects a man's fertility?

Male fertility depends on a healthy sperm shape, size, motility, and its concentration and count. The latter is often used as an indication of male fertility because many millions try to reach the egg but only one or few make it. They need to be strong swimmers.
Why do some healthy embryos fail to implant in the uterus?
These factors depend on other, underlying health conditions: Male infertility can be caused by weight gain, stress, poor sleep, smoking, microplastics and cannabis use.
Weight gain in particular effects the testes (also: testicles), which produce sperm and hormones like testosterone.
The testes function best at two degrees centigrade cooler than the rest of the body. Fat raises the temperature, and that can affect the sperm — its concentration, count and motility.
Why male infertility often goes undiagnosed

Male sexual health is often overlooked, possibly because men under the age of 40 don't generally have a regular reason to get checked — if you're older than 40, you may get your prostate checked annually. But even a urologist won't check your sperm count unless you ask them.
Women, on the other hand, get a monthly signal — their menstrual cycle — and may be able to infer from that that something is wrong.
A man gets no such natural signals about his fertility until he tries to conceive with a woman. And by then he may be 30 or 40, when some health outcomes are hard to reverse.
Riffat Bibi, a clinical embryologist who has led an IVF laboratory in Pakistan for 17 years, described what men often say on arrival: "Okay, check my wife first."
Sometimes a mother-in-law brings the daughter-in-law, which also suggests that the mother-in-law thinks: It can't be my son's fault.
And some patients "feel sexual activity is equivalent to fertility, which it is not," said Bibi.
Roughly 80% of Bibi's cases now involve a male factor, far above the 50-50 split long assumed, and her laboratory has had to adapt, she said.

They are also seeing this development in IVF (in vitro fertilization) treatment. Sperm has become so poor that nearly all her clients need an embryologist to pick a single sperm and inject it directly into the egg.
But there is another factor than many men don't talk about much: synthetic testosterone — or steroids.
IVF explained: Process, costs & risks
Testosterone shuts down sperm production
Some men, keen on a muscley body, suppress their own sperm production unknowingly by taking anabolic steroids, a synthetic form of testosterone.

The appeal of anabolic steroids is straightforward, said Harrison Pope, a Harvard Medical School researcher: Steroids enhance athletic performance. A steroid user, who drinks, smokes and skips half of his workouts can outperform a dedicated, clean athlete.
Pope, who has studied steroids for three decades, said "they are highly effective."
But what you gain in athletic performance, you lose in fertility, because an over-supply of testosterone can shut down sperm production.
A healthy body will keep testosterone levels in balance. Too little testosterone can also impede sperm production.
Sperm production can restart if you stop taking testosterone supplements, but Pope said it depends on your age, and much you were taking and for how long.
Occasional steroid users usually regain a "normal" sperm count. The World Health Organization considers a normal sperm count to be about 16 million sperm per milliliter of semen (or higher).
Heavy, long-term steroid users, meanwhile, often do not recover or return to normal sperm production.

Users typically take steroids in cycles – weeks on the drug, followed by a a break to let the body recover. But when Dutch researchers followed 100 men through one cycle of steroids and for a year after, they found two-thirds still had very low sperm counts, some had no sperm at all, and a year later, their counts had still not returned to normal.

Not everyone takes steroids, and yet falling sperm counts still occur. Take India, for example, where Chirag Bhandari, runs the Institute of Andrology and Sexual Health in Jaipur. Bhandari estimates that steroids account for less than 0.1% of the country's falling sperm counts. Overweight, heat-stress and smoking are usually the cause.

If a man is tested early, his sperm count will often return to normal within six to twelve months, both Bhandari and Bibi said. But the longer the problem goes undetected, the less likely that becomes.

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Global leaders are gathering in New York this week for the 81st UN general assembly and given the state of the world, it’s likely to be a lively one.
We are expecting to hear today from the US president, Donald Trump, Finland’s president Alexander Stubb, and France’s Emmanuel Macron (in his last UNGA appearance), among others.

Macron got to New York early and already held talks with Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy last night, possibly trying to mediate ahead of the pair’s closely watched meeting later today. Trump and Zelenskyy are expected to sit down together in the late afternoon or early evening.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy meeting with French president Emmanuel Macron in New York, USA. Photograph: Presidential Press Service Handout/EPA

blocks.text: Outside the main UNGA room, it will also be worth keeping an eye on Trump’s meeting with Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Jens-Frederik Nielsen as they meet to sign the new Greenland deal on Arctic security.
Expect potentially diverging interpretations of what the deal actually involves…

blocks.caption: Denmark’s prime minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland's government leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen visit the 9/11 memorial and Ground Zero in New York. Photograph: Mads Claus Rasmussen/AP

blocks.text: Separately, I will also keep an eye on events back in Europe as EU ambassadors meet in Brussels to discuss the latest Russia sanctions list with some controversial attempts to amend it and take some fairly well-known names out of it. More on that shortly.
Lots for us to cover today.
It’s Tuesday, 22 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 14m agoEU deadlocked over plans to remove two Russian billionaires from sanctions list
17m agoMorning opening: Welcome to New York

blocks.text: EU deadlocked over plans to remove two Russian billionaires from sanctions list

blocks.caption: Jennifer Rankin

blocks.text: Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels

The EU is deadlocked over a plan to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list as part of a bitterly disputed deal to keep broader restrictions in place on nearly 3,000 people and companies accused of enabling Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Russian president Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Russian businessman and founder of USM Holdings Alisher Usmanov during an awarding ceremony at the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia in 2018. Photograph: SPUTNIK/Reuters

blocks.text: Ambassadors from the EU’s 27 member states failed to reach agreement at a meeting early on Tuesday – their third session in around 24 hours on the topic. The senior diplomats will reconvene later today just hours ahead of a legal deadline.
Without an agreement sanctions on nearly 3,000 people and entities accused of supporting the war on Ukraine will lapse at the end of Tuesday 22 September.
The list includes Vladimir Putin, foreign minister Sergei Lavrov, Duma deputies, Russia’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex.
The EU can also agree a short-term extension pending a longer agreement and has already prolonged the deadline by one week. One diplomat suggested that was a likely outcome.
Latvia emerged as the last-minute block on an agreement. Like many member states the Baltic state has strong objections to the de-listings, which are demanded by France and Slovakia.

Latvia’s prime minister Andris Kulbergs tweeted late Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise – the de-listings of Usmanov and Fridman in exchange for a 36-month extension of the blacklist of nearly 3,000 names, far longer than the usual six-month rollover.
He said:
“Extending sanctions for 36 months would be the right step. However, the price for it must not be simply striking both individuals from the sanctions list. Latvia cannot accept SUCH an offer.”

blocks.caption: Latvian prime minister Andris Kulbergs attends the European Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi, Finland last week. Photograph: Kaisa Siren/EPA

blocks.text: He added that his foreign minister, Baiba Braže, would work with “Brussels and Paris to find a solution SUITABLE for Latvia’s interests. We will seek support in the EUROPEAN UNION for Latvia’s position”.

When details of the expected deal emerged on Monday, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said the delisting was “unacceptable and would send the wrong signal to Moscow at a time when pressure needs to increase”.

France infuriated and stunned EU member states by joining Slovakia’s populist government in petitioning for Usmanov’s de-listing earlier this month. France has told EU diplomats only that the delisting is on national security grounds. The Financial Times has reported that it is linked to a prisoner exchange deal with Azerbaijan involving the release of French nationals.

Azerbaijan, along with the Organisation of Turkic States, has previously lobbied western decision-makers to remove Usmanov from sanctions listings, describing him as “a renowned philanthropist” who has built bridges between the West, Central Asia and wider Turkic world. Slovakia began lobbying for Usmanov and fellow billionaire Mikhail Fridman to be removed from the EU sanctions list in the summer.
Luxembourg has argued that Fridman should come off the list, if Usmanov is removed. Fridman is seeking $16bn in damages from Luxembourg for freezing his assets.

articles.title: 'Swan Song': New book by Princess Diana's brother drops
articles.summary: A memoir penned by Charles Spencer on his older sister's life has been released, opening old royal wounds nearly three decades after Princess Diana's death.

image.caption: Diana died in 1997, aged 36, in a car crash in Paris as she was being chased by paparazziImage: John Stillwell/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Charles Spencer's book about his late sister Princess Diana's life and former marriage to Britain's now King Charles III hit bookstores on Tuesday.
The book titled "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" is being published globally by Penguin and has been translated into 12 languages.
The memoir triggered a royal row even before it went on sale, after some of its pre-published extracts — laden with Spencer's explosive claims — received a rare reaction and rebuttal from the king.
Charles Spencer, the 9th Earl Spencer, is Diana's younger brother and has long clashed with the royal House of Windsor over how they treated the princess.
What does Charles Spencer say in his memoir of Princess Diana?
In one of the claims that made a splash ahead the new book's release, Spencer accused Charles of sounding "giddily elated" and "like a lottery winner" when he had called him after Diana's death.

Spencer also writes that he had argued against plans for Charles and Diana's sons, William and Harry, to walk in their mother's funeral procession in 1997, saying that she would not have wanted them to go through that ordeal.
Spencer claims Charles "went ballistic" during the argument , telling him: "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough."
William was 15-years-old at the time and Harry was 12.
The world was moved by somber visuals of the young princes walking behind Diana's coffin.
How has King Charles III reacted to Spencer's claims?
Following the release of the book's excerpts last week, Buckingham Palace published a strongly-worded statement.

"His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said in a statement considered rare as far as responses from the royal household go.
Princess Diana's life and death
In 1981, a 20-year-old Lady Diana Spencer married a 32-year-old Charles, who was then the Prince of Wales, in a fairytale wedding that was televised globally.

Their whirlwind romance soon hit rock bottom and culminated in a public breakdown of their marriage. Diana famously told the BBC in an interview that "there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded" in reference to Charles' ⁠relationship with Camilla Parker ​Bowles.
Diana, known as the people's princess, was loved by people from all over the world. Her popularity led to her experiencing a media frenzy that lasted nearly all her adult life.
The royal couple divorced in 1996 and Diana died a year later, aged 36, in a car crash in Paris as she was being pursued by paparazzi.
Charles married Parker Bowles in 2005.

articles.title: Will Germany have enough gas this winter amid energy supply crunch?
articles.summary: Germany's gas storage sites are far less full than in recent years. Officials say supplies are secure, but analysts warn that a cold winter or import disruptions could push prices higher. So how…

image.caption: Compared to previous years, natural gas storage levels in Germany are lowImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: As of mid-September 2026, Germany had stored just about 141 terawatt-hours of gas, accounting for around 57% of the country's total storage capacity.
Last winter just under 134 terawatt-hours of gas were withdrawn from storage, according to the Federal Network Agency, the agency that monitors the country's electricity and gas networks.

At first glance, the numbers sounds reassuring, especially since last winter was quite cold and therefore required a lot of heating. But compared to previous years, natural gas storage levels are low.
On September 4, Markus Söder, the premier of Bavaria, called for intervention by the federal government.
Rising fuel prices put pressure on German drivers

A few days later, the opposition Green Party accused the economy minister of negligence. "The gas storage facilities are not full. We are facing a potential shortage," said Britta Hasselmann, co-leader of the Greens' parliamentary group.
Such statements have raised concerns about potential gas shortages in Germany this winter.

To assess the current situation, however, various factors such as imports and the diversification of supply sources need to be taken into account , not least since Germany is no longer as dependent on a single importer as it was on Russia until 2022.
Will Germany have enough gas?
Most experts interviewed by DW are not concerned about the winter gas supply.

Charlie Grüneberg, spokesperson for the German Gas and Hydrogen Industry association, points to the contracts that have been signed for the medium term. "Anyone who has contractually secured their gas needs for the winter with a reliable supplier will receive the agreed quantities," he said.
Sebastian Heinermann, managing director of INES, a German association for gas and hydrogen storage system operators, is more cautious.

He pointed out that it's technically possible to fill gas storage facilities in Germany to around 77%, but this would require filling at a level that "has not been observed even once in the past three weeks," Heinermann said. "If this trend continues unchanged, the fill level will reach only about 65% by November 1."

blocks.caption: Most natural gas is stored underground at facilities like these in Jemgum on the Lower EmsImage: Astora

blocks.text: Still, the Federal Network Agency sees no cause for concern.

"The gas supply in Germany is stable," the agency's spokesperson, Nadia Affani, told DW. "Security of supply is currently guaranteed. Based on the latest information, the Federal Network Agency continues to assess the risk of a gas supply crunch as low."

Germany's Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy shared a similar assessment. The ministry "is monitoring all developments very closely to ensure security of supply. There are currently no signs of a supply shortage," said spokesperson Susanne Ungrad.
Officials downplay supply risks

She also pointed to an array of factors that determine the price of natural gas like available storage, ongoing imports via pipelines and LNG terminals, demand and the situation on the international energy markets.
"We are prepared for further developments," Ungrad stressed.
Grüneberg also takes a more holistic view.
"The key factor is whether enough gas can be procured and transported to and through Germany. Supply contracts, storage facilities, pipeline imports and LNG are all interlinked," he underscored.
"Thanks to investments in LNG terminals, new import routes and reverse-flow capabilities, the infrastructure is now significantly more robust than it was in 2022."
Gas prices rise ahead of winter
As the winter approaches and people start heating their homes more, gas prices tend to climb. This trend is already evident, said Heinermann.
"In the second quarter, the gas price across various contracts on the futures market stood at around €46 ($52) per megawatt-hour. Recently, the gas price has risen to over €80."

Olaf Geyer from the US consulting firm Arthur D. Little, who has been monitoring the German market, said there is no immediate supply problem, but: "If the winter turns out to be cold or there are disruptions on the import side, prices could rise quickly."
Grüneberg said "reliable price forecasts" are difficult to make and noted that low storage levels could cause prices to rise "if additional volumes have to be procured on the market."

However, there are no signs of a shortage on the supply side. "As things stand today, there are no indications of a physical shortage of supply by the end of winter. The futures markets are not signaling this at the moment either," said Grüneberg.
Can Germany refit gas pipelines to transport cleaner energy?
The German economy ministry points out that "the prices currently quoted for forward contracts for the winter are only slightly higher than the spot market prices for immediate transactions."
"The usual summer-winter spread, which made it economically viable to store gas during the summer months, was therefore not present," it added.

The "spread" is based on the principle of buying gas cheaply in summer and selling it at higher prices in winter. This year, gas prices rose following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, undermining that seasonal pattern.
How to refill storage faster
Geyer, who also focuses on the summer-winter spread, said storage facilities aren't fuller this time round because it hasn't been economically viable.

"For the future, we need better incentives for filling storage facilities — and risk management on the part of utilities that looks not only at the purchase price but also at how much actual consumption can deviate from projections," he underlined.
Heinermann also called for effective economic incentives to fill gas storage facilities.

"In the medium term, Germany needs a reliable market framework that, through incentives, obligations or a combination of both, ensures sufficient storage levels on a long-term basis while preserving as much market-based flexibility as possible."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Australia investigating how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for US went missing in Hong Kong
articles.summary: Disappearance of jet components sparks concern some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed

blocks.text: Richard Marles says the Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong.

The acting prime minister said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” will be reviewed, however, he claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.

The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.

The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.

“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained on of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The Guardian has contacted the Pentagon.

While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.

“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.

Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence community that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.

More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F3-5 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

articles.title: How will Germany's Merz respond after crushing state election results and losses to the far right?
articles.summary: Germany's far-right AfD and the socialist Left Party gained ground in recent state elections, while the centrist parties lost support. The biggest loser is Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz is under pressure following the election defeats in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western PomeraniaImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: Why have the results of the two German state elections held on Sunday, September 20, thrown the spotlight on the federal government led by the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its chancellor Friedrich Merz?

For the first time, the party failed to reach the required 5% of votes to enter parliament in the northeastern coastal state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. It marks the first time in its history that the CDU has failed to enter a state parliament. In the city-state of Berlin, where the CDU was incumbent, the party suffered heavy losses and is likely to end up on the opposition benches.

The chancellor says he is aware of the significance. "This election is a profound turning point. It is a dramatic and unprecedented result for the CDU in Germany that we could not clear the 5% threshold. For an entire bloc to leave the state parliament is a heavy blow, and that will resonate with us for a long time to come," he said.
German state elections reveal increasingly polarized country

At the same time, Merz conceded that federal policy, which had failed to convince the public, had played a role in the defeats. Most voters are also not satisfied with the chancellor himself. However, he also sees another cause: "We are experiencing a dramatic shift of the party-political system in Germany, as are many other countries," Merz said.

The chancellor pointed to the competition at the political margins: "In [Sunday's] elections, more than 40% of the vote went to forces which are destructive, which question our political, parliamentary system. And who attempt to excite people with radical and simple solutions," was his analysis. Merz did not name the parties he was referring to, but he clearly meant the Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the Left Party.

The AfD is classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency, in five of Germany's 16 federal states — but not in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, both regions in which it was able to significantly grow its share of the vote.

In the German capital, the AfD's result grew from 9% to 16% compared to the previous election. In the northeastern coastal state, the party more than doubled its result, to 38%. AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said, alluding to his party's color: "The blue wave cannot be stopped."
Criticism of the CDU's 'firewall' policy

The AfD's other co-leader Alice Weidel, concluded that the CDU had been pulverized and that the chancellor's resignation is "overdue." "This clearly shows that we have replaced the CDU as the party of the masses," she said.

"That is also the result of a very unintelligent firewall policy," Weidel added, referring to the CDU's so-called resolution of incompatibility, which rejects coalitions with both her party and the socialist Left.

The AfD's claim to have taken the place of the CDU is unfounded, according to political scientist Wolfgang Muno from the University of Rostock in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The AfD is no big tent party representing conservative interests, he told DW: "It is a right-wing extremist party which has managed to bring together various groups."

Muno's opinion of the Left Party is vastly different to Merz's: "We have seen that the Left has really moved toward being a pragmatic, democratically oriented party. Therefore, there is no reason for the Christian Democrats to simply accuse them of being extremists, because the Left is not an extremist party," Muno said.
The Left Party faces antisemitism allegations

Muno considers criticism of Israeli policies legitimate. At the same time, he notes that it had been accompanied by antisemitic incidents . He expects the Left to send a clear signal that such things are not acceptable. "But not being open to cooperating with a democratic Left Party is, in my opinion, a bad sign," he said, referring to the CDU.

In Berlin, the socialist Left with lead candidate Elif Eralp succeeded in doubling its previous result to 26% and won an election in the city-state for the first time. A scandalous campaign event appearance by rapper Dahabflex, who sang about wishing death for Israel's soldiers, appears not to have damaged the party. Its district association in Neukölln, which had invited the singer, said it intended to clarify the matter.

Josef Schuster, President of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, is skeptical: "So far there have been no personnel or political consequences." He appealed to the Social Democrats and Greens not to form a coalition with the Berlin election winners.

Federal co-leader of the Left, Ines Schwerdtner, told DW that she would not tolerate antisemitism among the party's ranks. "We are there in Berlin to build bridges — Elif Eralp is doing that. And within the party we will absolutely ensure that something like this does not happen."

Eralp, whose parents fled to Germany after a military coup in Turkey, could become the first mayor from the Left in Berlin. About 200,000 of the German capital's four million residents have Turkish roots.

Against this background, the lead candidate considers her and her party's success as an important sign: "I view this election result also as a victory for solidarity, for diversity, for democracy, against the shift to the right which we are experiencing in many places in this country," she said.
Why Germany's political center is losing ground
Merz vows to push through with welfare reforms

Manuela Schwesig, the Social Democrats' (SPD) lead candidate in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, scored a partial success. With about 36% of the vote, her party came in just behind the AfD, but she has good prospects of being able to remain state premier: "I will propose to my party that we hold talks with both the Greens and the Left — the two democratic parties represented in the state parliament — and fulfil our electoral mandate," she said.

The incumbent, who has held the office since 2017, is critical of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's announcement that he wants to press on with his course of deep cuts to the welfare system. The most controversial is the planned pension reform. "He is misjudging the situation of what the people on the ground think, at least in my state," Schwesig said.

She reminded Merz of the agreement his party made with the SPD at the federal level: "I would like for the coalition to implement exactly what we negotiated together in the coalition agreement, namely that the pension without deductions remains possible after 45 years of contribution."
This agreement is currently hanging in the balance. Like the SPD's Schwesig, some eastern German CDU state premiers have spoken out against the chancellor's plans.

Despite this, the SPD faces a dilemma because at the federal level it is part of the government with the CDU. The party's co-leader, Bärbel Bas , now wants to draw the "correct conclusions" from the results of the state parliament elections.

However, she also said that the party had taken responsibility in the federal government. "We are in this coalition, and we also want to maintain it. Nevertheless, we must also accept the analysis from the campaign trail that the people are not satisfied with the upcoming reforms. That means that we, together with our coalition partner, must seek solutions."
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Princess Diana's brother makes explosive claims about royals in new memoir
articles.summary: Here are some of the key revelations from Charles Earl Spencer's highly anticipated memoir "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister." It has already provoked Buckingham Palace to react.

image.caption: Princess Diana's fatal car crash happened nearly 30 years ago, in August 1997Image: John Shelley Collection/LFI/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the new book "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," Charles Spencer, the 9th Earl Spencer, offers his perspective on the life of his late sister, Diana, Princess of Wales.

As British tabloid culture ensures that every feud and controversy linked to the royal family gets amplified into a major public debate, the memoir started making headlines before its publication on September 22.

Among some of the key revelations of the book, he says that he believes that Diana had ADHD, and that "as part of that condition she suffered from Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria," which he describes as "an intense emotional pain in the face of others' rejection or criticism."

Spencer also claims their father developed a "romantic connection" with the future Queen Elizabeth II, until he was warned off her by Lord Mountbatten, who was the maternal uncle and close mentor of the queen's husband, Prince Philip.
But most polemically, Spencer revisits one of the British royal family's most painful chapters: the aftermath of Diana's tragic death in a car crash on August 31, 1997.

blocks.caption: 'Swan Song: Diana, My Sister' has been translated into 12 languages for its global release on September 22Image: Penguin Random House/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: 'We'll forget her soon enough'
Spencer writes that when Queen Elizabeth II first heard of Diana's accident, her initial reaction was: "What is she up to now?" before the gravity of the situation became clear.

Diana's death sparked a global outpouring of grief. In the aftermath of the car crash, the royals faced strong public backlash for their delayed and cold response to the tragedy. The Queen's first public address came five days after Diana's death.

In his book, Spencer suggests that some inside Buckingham Palace were "relieved — indeed pleased" that she had died. He also recounts a phone conversation with King Charles, then-Prince of Wales that happened days after her death. According to Spencer, the prince sounded "giddily elated — like a lottery winner."

Spencer writes that they discussed how he objected to having Prince William, then 15, and Prince Harry, then 12, walk behind their mother's coffin during the funeral procession at the internationally televised funeral.

Spencer felt it would be traumatic to put the boys in the media spotlight just after their mother had died. He writes in the book that he believes the boys were used as a protective shield for Charles, as Buckingham Palace officials feared "members of the public might shout abuse at him," whereas the children's presence "would surely guarantee against insults flying."

blocks.caption: From left to right: Earl Spencer, Prince William, Prince Harry and Prince Charles following the coffin to the funeral of Diana, Princess of Wales in 1997Image: Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: Spencer also recounts Diana's belief that Prince Charles had already become jealous of her popularity decades earlier.

He describes how Prince Charles went into a "stream of anger" during the phone conversation after her death. The princess's brother writes that her former husband unleashed "his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough!'"

But nearly 30 years after the fatal car crash, Diana remains a global icon. The 36-year-old was a glamorous celebrity, renowned for her advocacy for different causes, including her groundbreaking support for AIDS patients.

Buckingham Palace directly reacted to the first excerpt published in the Daily Mail: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle. His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss."

In contrast, the Palace met Prince Harry's accusations in his 2023 memoir "Spare" with total institutional silence, applying the royals' traditional public relations strategy of "Never complain, never explain."
Speaking on behalf of the 'blood family'
The feud between Earl Spencer and Buckingham Palace is not new.

Spencer famously delivered a passionate eulogy for his sister at Westminster Abbey in 1997. In it, he not only criticized the role of the paparazzi in the accident, calling his sister the "most hunted person of the modern age," but also set himself apart from the royals by referring to his blood ties with Diana in a promise to protect her boys "from a similar fate."

"I pledge that we, your blood family, will do all we can to continue the imaginative way in which you were steering these two exceptional young men so that their souls are not simply immersed by duty and tradition but can sing openly as you planned," he said at the time.

blocks.caption: Charles Spencer, 9th Earl Spencer, has sparked a highly publicized feud with the royal family with his new memoirImage: Jordan Pettitt/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: On the day of the funeral, Spencer writes, Queen Elizabeth II offered through intermediaries to posthumously restore Diana's "Her Royal Highness" (HRH) title. Spencer declined, as he felt the gesture had little meaning after her death.
Even though Buckingham Palace has always insisted Diana gave up the title voluntarily, Spencer writes that she was left "dreadfully hurt" by its removal amid her divorce with Charles.
Intrusive tabloid culture led to her death
In his book, Spencer returns to the themes he addressed in his eulogy, accusing the editors and publishers who bought intrusive photos of Diana of having contributed to killing his sister.
According to him, British tabloid culture turned into system that profited from Diana's suffering and encouraged increasingly extreme invasions of privacy.

After the divorce, large sections of the media began portraying Diana as unstable, manipulative, difficult or attention-seeking. Paparazzi would provoke distress and photograph her reaction; newspapers would then publish stories suggesting she was unstable.

She was unable to escape media scrutiny, making her extremely unhappy: "It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all," Spencer writes, adding: "Her love for her sons stopped her from going further."
A lucrative release ahead of 30th anniversary of Diana's death

While Spencer has long criticized the destructive nature of the British tabloid system, the promotion of his memoir relies on the exact ecosystem he decries. He has sold serialization rights of the book to the UK's Daily Mail — one of the very tabloid outlets frequently associated with intense royal scrutiny.

blocks.caption: According to her brother, Diana already knew on her wedding day that the man she was marrying did not truly love herImage: AFP

blocks.text: Some critics accuse him of wanting to cash in on the tragedy, with the high-profile book published just ahead of the 30th anniversary of Diana's death.

His supporters however feel that Diana's brother is justified to share his personal perspective on their shared experience, noting that many other authors have profited off her legacy over the decades.

Spencer has stated that his account aims to correct decades of "untruths that have become accepted over time" and inaccurate portrayals of his late sister by outside biographers and commentators over the years.

"At heart, this is a brother's simple tribute to an extraordinary sister," Earl Spencer wrote of his own work on Instagram, adding, "A month ago I read 'Swan Song' out, over three days, for a recording so that it could be available on audiobook. When I finished the recording, I thought: 'That is exactly what I wanted and needed to say — and she would, I reckon, have approved of every word.'"

articles.title: Middle East crisis live: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warns it will ‘change geography of war’ if US escalates conflict
articles.summary:
The US president said in an interview ahead of the United Nations meeting that he was considering ‘wiping Iran out’

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps warned it would “change the geography of…

blocks.text: IRGC warns it will 'change the geography of the war' if US escalates the conflict
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps warned it would “change the geography of the war” if the US escalates the conflict, after Donald Trump issued fresh threats against the Islamic Republic.

In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Trump said “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future”, adding that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.

A spokesperson for the IRGC, Hossein Mohebbi, responded with a warning that if the US were to launch fresh attacks against Iran, Tehran would use “new weapons with capabilities into the battle”. “If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Mohebbi was quoted as having said.
“Our targets will no longer necessarily be the same as before,” he said, according to the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting, adding that Iran has targets that have not yet been struck.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump is wrestling with an unpopular war and low approval ratings ahead of November’s US midterm elections. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters

blocks.text: The comments come as the US and Iran remain locked in an impasse over the strait of Hormuz and after attacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.

The Houthis, who operate independently of Iran’s instructions, have seized territory along the country’s Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping route that links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal.

The Houthis have also attacked oil facilities and other types of infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, in response for Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. The attacks have further disrupted energy markets, pushing up global fuel prices, including in the US, where consumers have been hit hard.

Iran hugely benefits from the Houthis fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on the US to relent over Iran, which has insisted it will not allow the reopening of the strait of Hormuz until all its conditions have been met.
With diplomatic negotiations stalled, traffic in the strait continues to be severely disrupted, with Iran firing on commercial ships and demanding it first approve passage along its authorised route.
In response, the US, which started the war on Iran alongside Israel in February, is maintaining a counter-blockade of Iranian ports while intensifying economic pressure.
The US has also fired on commercial shipping in the region and has killed Iranian civilians in its strikes.

articles.summary: While India is fuming over a viral video of two minors being harassed in Bihar, a case of an alleged gang-rape of a minor has emerged in a posh Delhi neighborhood. Meanwhile, India's foreign minister…

image.caption: Police are looking into the incident, where the attackers are believed to have posed as security personnel [FILE: Sept 22, 2026]Image: Francis Mascarenhas/REUTERS

blocks.text: While India is fuming over a viral video of two minors being harassed in Bihar, a case of an alleged gang-rape of a minor has emerged in a posh Delhi neighborhood. Meanwhile, India's foreign minister is at the UNGA.

blocks.caption: Police are looking into the incident, where the attackers are believed to have posed as security personnel [FILE: Sept 22, 2026]Image: Francis Mascarenhas/REUTERS

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Delhi police look into report regarding a minor who was allegedly gang-raped in New Delhi
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar urges multilateralism at UNGA in New York

blocks.text: Here's a roundup of the headlines from India on Tuesday, September 22:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
September 22, 2026
Minor allegedly gang-raped in South Delhi neighborhood
A 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped by three men posing as policemen in New Delhi on Monday evening, authorities said on Tuesday.
The girl had been visiting a temple in southeast Delhi with a male friend, before they both retreated to a nearby park.

There, they were intercepted by three men who claimed to be police officers, authorities said, as reported by Hindustan Times. One of the accused is said to have held the male friend down while the girl was gang-raped. The men also reportedly threatened the duo with arrest if they reported the assault. The incident took place at about 7:30 p.m. local time (0200 GMT).

The Police received a call about the incident soon after and reached the spot, taking the girl for a medical examination. Authorities have launched a formal investigation under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO) and the Indian criminal law and teams were deployed to trace the accused.
Ten years after Delhi gang rape, has anything changed?

One of the three accused of the gang-rape fired three shots at the police as they attempted to arrest him. During the exchange, one of the bullets struck an officer's bulletproof vest. The accused was shot in his right leg before he was arrested, news agency Press Trust of India reported.

The news of the Delhi gang-rape comes a day after a viral video from the eastern state of Bihar surfaced on social media, showing a group of about seven men molesting a minor girl while assaulting her male companion. The video has enraged netizens and political leaders alike.
Delhi remains one of the least safe cities for women in India, according to the National Annual Report and Index on Women's safety 2025.

articles.title: ‘What we have is unique’: the Indian craftsmanship behind global luxury fashion
articles.summary:
Generations of artisans from Mumbai to Lucknow have shaped the world’s most coveted designs. Plus, the gen Z memes giving classic Bollywood a new life

The

blocks.text: The zardozi embroidery on a Dior dress, the T-strap leather sandals at a Prada show, the mirror-work technique used on a Fendi bag – for decades, the skill of Indian artisans has been an invisible force behind some of the world’s most coveted fashion.
Now, that work is beginning to claim its own place in the spotlight, and the Mumbai-based textile and embroidery atelier Chanakya International is at the forefront.

Chanakya marked its 40th anniversary this month, celebrating with three exhibitions that trace its journey from an embroidery powerhouse to a present-day craft and cultural institution. The person steering it is 49-year-old Karishma Swali, whose father set up the group’s operations in the 1980s.

“What we have as a country is unique,” she tells me of India’s rich textile and craft heritage. “It’s unparalleled in many ways, and it’s the only place where we continue to practise it.” During the Renaissance, she says, France and Italy had established and varied traditions. “But what we have in India today is [what] other parts of the world have lost.”

Chanakya has a network of 1,400 artisans, and says that some are 13th-generation craftspeople, skilled in hundreds of embroidery traditions and supplying almost every luxury label you can imagine. Among the techniques they have revived is the Mughal-era silver filigree lace, or chaand jaal, reintroduced in a lighter form that has since become a regular feature in couture collections.

In 2023, Dior held a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India, showcasing its partnership with Chanakya, in a high-profile acknowledgment of Indian craftsmanship. The runway saw sari-inspired skirts, vibrant madras-checks sets and Nehru-collar jackets.

These collaborations are supported by expert craft knowledge passed down and refined over generations, and they need institutional support to survive. The Kalhath Institute, a craft-preservation centre in Lucknow, runs residencies that pair artists from across the world with local artisans.

Kalhath’s co-founder Mohammed Amine Dadda tells me that Indian craftsmanship’s defining quality is “intelligence of the hand” – a sensitive, slow and cumulative process underpinned by patience and dexterity. “Without this technical mastery, and the considerable time required to create the most demanding pieces, haute couture and contemporary luxury simply could not bring their most ambitious creative visions to life.”

This mastery is not limited to textiles. When it comes to jewellery, global luxury brands have long sought Jaipur-based the Gem Palace, established in 1852 by the Kasliwal family, who still run it today. Samarth Kasliwal, 33, says part of the appeal lies in the visual language of Indian artistry itself. “There is something about Indian artistry that is inspired by nature,” he tells me, pointing to the recurring use of floral patterns and animals across Indian art and design. These motifs are universal, and travel across the lines of culture and language.

One recent collaboration Kasliwal is particularly proud of is a collection for Dior featuring green onyx and rock crystals, with engravings of birds, animals and flowers. The combination, he says, is reminiscent of traditional Indian jewellery, while drawing on techniques that remain central to the atelier’s work today.

blocks.caption: Jaipur-based Gem Palace has worked with the French fashion house Dior on a jewellery collection. Photograph: Courtesy of Gem Palace and Dior

blocks.text: With increased visibility, the question of credit and appropriation has become harder to ignore. Last week, a Ralph Lauren gown from the designer’s spring 2027 collection attracted criticism after many Indians pointed out that the embroidery the brand described as “embellishments” looked a lot like Indian zardozi, but without any accompanying credit. (Ralph Lauren did not respond to my request for comment.)

Then, Fendi came under fire when people noticed that a baguette bag from its autumn/winter collection featured mirrorwork often seen in Gujarati crafts. In April, Fendi credited Chanakya artisans in a social media video showcasing the same embroidery. But the product description on its site failed to mention any Indian inspiration, and its final label read “Made in Italy”.

After I asked Fendi about the discrepancy, the brand cited its “creative partnership” with Chanakya of more than three decades, saying it “remains committed to supporting and recognizing India’s rich craft heritage”. The website descriptor now reads: “Made in Italy and India with Chanakya”.
A recent Financial Times report noted that under EU rules, garments embroidered in India can still end up with a European label – so long as the final construction and finishing take place in Europe.

Last year, Prada was accused of appropriating Indian culture with Kolhapuri-inspired sandals, a controversy that showed us these debates around recognition can sometimes produce a more structural response. “We acknowledge the sandals … are inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear, with a centuries-old heritage,” Lorenzo Bertelli, the corporate social responsibility chief at the Italian fashion house, had written in a letter to the Maharashtra chamber of commerce at the time.

Prada subsequently partnered with state-backed organisations in Maharashtra and Karnataka to produce a limited-edition collection, Made in India, and committed to a three-year training programme for artisans specialising in the craft.

blocks.caption: Karishma Swali with Chanakya School of Craft students. Photograph: Hashim Badani/ Chanakya International

blocks.text: Might these collaborations, controversies and corrections represent a shift in India’s place in the fashion industry? Anthropologist Phyllida Jay, author of Inspired by India: How India Transformed Global Design, appears to think so, placing the debate in a longer arc. “The stories of the ateliers producing highly skilled Indian craft in the elevated realm of European luxury and high fashion is part of a broader paradigm shift,” she writes, “where over 70 years after the end of colonial rule, India is being looked at in a different way on the world stage.” It is, in a way, a reversal, moving from a colonial history of extraction toward one in which Indians themselves get a voice in how their craft is represented.

Swali is ensuring this visibility also lives on through the Chanakya School of Craft, which she set up in 2016. Its 18-month programme provides free embroidery training and a travel honorarium to dozens of women, some of whom have gone on to work at the main atelier. Others have set up their own independent studios.

I had a chance to visit the space – inside a high-rise in Lower Parel, where those as young as 18 learn intricate needlework alongside grandmothers in their 60s. “Craft in India has never been institutionalised,” Swali says of the ethos behind the initiative. “It’s intergenerational,” she says, adding that women have often been excluded.

India’s culture of craft has always been precious. Growing up, I loved having the choice to affordably create any type of clothing. At one point, I had a small army of tailors, each with a different specialisation, whom I’d go to for different needs. I’d buy ajrakh and mashru silks from Dastkar or Nalli, and hand it to the right Masterji to stitch, embroider and tweak to my size. So, to me, Indian craftsmanship is not just a part of luxury, but a luxury itself.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: Time Out has named Mumbai’s Bandra West one of the coolest neighbourhoods in the world. Photograph: Danto Production

blocks.text: Travel | Time Out just confirmed what everyone in Mumbai’s Bandra West knows: that it’s one of the coolest neighbourhoods in the world. The other Indian spot to make the cut is Delhi’s food and fashion centre, Humayunpur. The top spot went to Jongno 3-ga in Seoul – my second home!
after newsletter promotion

Business | India will levy a 0.4% charge on merchants for UPI payments above Rs 2,000, starting on 15 October. The charges will not be applicable when the payment is made from one person to another. Ashneer Grover, co-founder and former CEO of fintech firm BharatPe slammed the move, describing it as “tax collection”.

Immigration | An investigation by Scroll’s Rokibuz Zaman has revealed a troubling pattern in West Bengal: since June, at least nine Muslim men and two children have been picked up by the police from their homes over allegations that they are Bangladeshi nationals – without being given a chance to prove their citizenship. Most were picked up and detained in midnight raids, the report said, and family members accused the police of not producing warrants.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Fashion designer Payal Khandwala recommends the perfect saree weave. Photograph: Payal Khandwala

blocks.text: Fashion designer Payal Khandwala, whose spring-summer ’26 collection featured handwoven silks, cottons and brocades, recommends the perfect saree weave: “The delicate poetry of a Jamdani saree is definitely my favourite. A 2,000-year-old craft, typically woven in fine muslin and of Bengali origin, it’s somewhat an unsung hero. The weaving process itself is exceptionally intricate. Using a supplementary weft technique, thousands of markings are meticulously mapped on to the warp to recreate the pattern, interlaced by hand with a wooden shuttle and metallic needle to guide the motifs in silver and gold yarn, on fine mulberry silk and organza.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Foreign portfolio investors have pulled out £1.2bn from Indian equities. Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters

blocks.text: Foreign investors have pulled out Rs 13,138 crore (£1.02bn) from Indian equities in the first half of September, wiping out about half of the net inflows recorded in August.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Old Bollywood, new jokes … the memes giving classic film stills a gen Z makeover. Photograph: Bahaish Kapoor

blocks.text: The true measure of my love for my friends is in the number of memes I send them. One of the accounts I rely on is Bahaish Kapoor’s. The screenwriter-turned-meme evangelist pairs black-and-white Bollywood stills with contemporary gen Z sass, and lets incongruity do the rest. What makes an image meme-worthy? “I always look for people who are in a deep philosophical, romantic, dramatic action moment which I can repurpose to bring in a whole new meaning,” he tells me. “I try to mix and match and see what’s working.” His 340,000-plus followers include Sharon Stone and Hrithik Roshan.

“I just want to make people feel a little better,” says Kapoor, adding that he receives a lot of DMs from people about how his page helped them through a bad day. “People confessing that they are lighter because of this experience is all that I can hope for. I mean, that’s the endgame.”
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
articles.summary: In New York, the prime minister will also deliver a speech to the UN General Assembly expected to be focused on AI.

blocks.text: Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.
The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.
The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship".

"We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it."
Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".

Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).

He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."
The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".
He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.
His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.

For a new British prime minister, the first meeting with a US president has always been a pivotal encounter, but officials are well aware of the added jeopardy of a public appearance alongside the most unpredictable president in American history.
In advance of the meeting, the UK revealed that the UK and the US have, for the first time, fired an American torpedo from a British undersea drone in a military exercise.
The torpedo, described as "heavyweight" by UK officials, is "designed to sink ships and deep diving submarines", Downing Street said.
It was launched in UK waters last week from a 12-metre long undersea drone called Excalibur, made in Plymouth.

It is the first time either the UK or the US have launched a torpedo from an uncrewed underwater vessel, rather than a crewed submarine, and is seen as a breakthrough in attempts to protect vital infrastructure such as deep sea data cables.
"Our work together already shows what can be achieved when our two countries combine our expertise and innovation," the prime minister said.
Burnham was also asked by reporters about the UK government seeking to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.
It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.
Burnham spoke to the Mauritian prime minister, Navin Ramgoolam, on Monday.
He was asked by reporters to outline what he had told Ramgoolam, whether he supported the deal and if he had a plan to convince Trump to back it.
Burnham replied: "I said that we remain determined to secure the long-term operation of the base, which is crucial to our security and that of our allies.
"The assurance I gave was I will work towards a resolution, at the moment we don't have that, but I gave an assurance that I would commit to working towards one."

articles.title: Iran must stop arming Houthis in Yemen, G7 says ahead of UN General Assembly
articles.summary: The G7 also condemns "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying that the escalation in fighting in Yemen jeopardises global energy security.

blocks.text: Iran must "end its arming of and support" for the Houthis in Yemen, the foreign ministers of G7 nations have said in a joint statement.

The G7 also condemned "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, adding that the recent escalation in fighting against Saudi-backed forces in Yemen represented a threat to regional and global energy security.

Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after the Iran-backed group seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a critical shipping route for global trade.
The statement comes ahead of the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where senior Iranian officials are due to speak.

"We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith," said the foreign ministers of the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.

It went on: "Their reprehensible actions constitute a dangerous pattern of escalation that risks further exacerbating the conflict, undermining international trade and creating global economic instability."

"Looking forward, we will continue to support the legitimate Government of Yemen and reaffirm our strong commitment to the unity, sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Yemen," the ministers said.
Their statement was issued following a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Saudi Arabia has retaliated with hundreds of air strikes in the region.
The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia, including the capital city, Riyadh.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, involving a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus.
Burnham said the announcement followed a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
A diplomatic source told AFP that France has pledged support as well, and says is ready to work on "securing" Saudi energy infrastructure via a "strictly defensive approach".
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also requested military support from President Donald Trump, US media reported.
Trump has wavered for weeks over whether to act on a Saudi request for help in fighting the Houthis, the New York Times reported on Monday.
The US president had earlier told Fox News that he was in "deciding mode" as he considered options for the next steps in the war against Iran.
On Sunday, US embassies across the Middle East issued new security alerts as fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed coalition in Yemen intensified.
The Houthis declare themselves to be part of the Iranian-led "axis of resistance" against Israel, the US and the wider West - along with armed group such as Hamas and Lebanon's Hezbollah movement.
Tehran has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.
